written_by_Rachael.Original: I did not want to finish the year because I know that as the days pass, as January becomes February and February becomes summer, certain things will happen. My image of John at the instant of his death will become less immediate, less raw. It will become something that happened in another year. My sense of John himself, John alive, will become more remote, even “mudgy,” softened, transmuted into whatever best serves my life without him. In fact this is already beginning to happen. All year I have been keeping time by last year’s calendar: what were we doing on this day last year, where did we have dinner, is it the day a year ago we flew to Honolulu after Quintana’s wedding, is it the day a year ago we flew back from Paris, is it the day. I realized today for the first time that my memory of this day a year ago is a memory that does not involve John. This day a year ago was December 31, 2003. John did not see this day a year ago. John was dead.I was crossing Lexington Avenue when this occurred to me.I know why we try to keep the dead alive: we try to keep them alive in order to keep them with us.I also know that if we are to live ourselves there comes a point at which we must relinquish the dead, let them go, keep them dead.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.
written_by_Rachael.Reason: The original is written in Didion's signature, matter-of-fact, somewhat affectless tone, with lines like: "I realized today for the first time that my memory of this day a year ago is a memory that does not involve John." For this reason, Excerpt 2 is more accurate in its emulation of voice and style. Excerpt 2 contains simple, poignant, but somewhat bare sentences like "After death, we cling to empty air" and "Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch." Meanwhile, Excerpt 1 is a bit more flowery and overwritten, with emotional lines like "The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow' and "The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment."

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: When I think of John now, whether in grief or joy, time makes a mirage of our parting. Memories are distant, those vibrant, vivid images inevitably softened by the passing days and nights into muddy and distorted reflections. My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. When he was alive, who did we see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then? Crossing Lexington Avenue in the wintry haze enveloping New York, a cold, damp curtain hung above the city, I come across the date—December 31, 2003—and realize John never saw this day last year. My exercise for keeping time has expired, and my husband lives in the distant past. I might transplant him here, invite him as memory into this moment to maintain our profound connection, the sort unsevered by death so long as he is kept within the perfect safety of memory. Yet it occurs to me—in this exercise of resurrection, I am only ensuring that I, too, never see December 31, 2003. That I, like John, live only in my recollections. Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: The air in the apartment is heavy, thick with the scent of lilies and the ghost of his presence.  Time, that relentless tide, keeps moving, yet I seem stranded, caught in the undertow of grief.  It's been a year and four months since John, my John, slipped through the veil, and the world insists on reminding me.The calendar, that cruel arbiter of time, mocks me with its relentless march forward.  Each day is a faded echo of the one before, a year removed.  I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.Yesterday, I crossed Lexington Avenue, the same way I've done a thousand times before.  But this time, it was different.  This time, I carried the weight of December 31, 2003, a date that exists in my world but not in his.  It was the day he ceased to be, the day the world shifted on its axis.And in that moment, I realized the terrible truth.  We who are left behind, we try to keep the dead alive in our memories, clinging to their fading essence like a lifeline.  But in doing so, we create a purgatory, a liminal space where they are neither here nor there.  To truly live, to move forward, we must keep them dead.  It's a harsh reality, a bitter pill to swallow.  But it's the only way to navigate the treacherous terrain of grief.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: I thought that the diction and register of Excerpt 2 was closer to the original. Excerpt 1 begins with a much more advanced, poetic vocabulary ("the mirage of our parting") whereas Excerpt 2 and the original start with very simple, direct vocabulary. The idea of "keeping time by last year's calendar" was also better expressed in Excerpt 2 through folding in John and the narrator in relation to the calendar and the narrator's speculations (I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.), and Excerpt 1 seemed to have introduced that same idea as a concern than folding it into the character's point of view.(My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. However, the refrain and sentimentality of John being dead was insisted upon in Excerpt 1 through its use of words like, or related to life and death towards the end ("Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead") which is similar to the original ("I know why we try to keep the dead alive: we try to keep them alive in order to keep them with us.I also know that if we are to live ourselves there comes a point at which we must relinquish the dead, let them go, keep them dead") whereas Excerpt 2 ended on a very general note ("To truly live, to move forward, we must keep them dead. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: It is December 31, 2004, and I find myself at the intersection of memory and absence, crossing Lexington Avenue on a day John never knew. The light changes, the traffic hums, but the world feels displaced, as though operating on a parallel timeline I can no longer inhabit. I ask myself where we were this day a year ago, but the question folds into itself, unanswered. There was no "we" then. There is no "we" now. It is just me, standing on the edge of a moment I never thought would arrive, tethered to someone who no longer exists in the present tense.Time has turned traitorous, reshaping vivid recollections into something blurred, soft-edged, mudgy. I want the sharpness back—the sound of his voice calling my name, the exact tilt of his head when he laughed—but instead I am left with echoes that refuse to hold their shape. For months I kept time through him: what we ate, where we sat, how the hours unfolded a year ago. That tether, too, is breaking, and I know it must. To live is to keep the dead where they belong, not erased but sequestered, a layer beneath the surface of everything we do and feel. I loved him, love him still, but loving him has become the act of holding his absence, acknowledging the permanence of it, walking forward through the days he will never know. This is the life left, the one that does not wait.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Since John’s death, my memories (of him, but also of most things), once acute, have become soft and mudgy. For a while, I was able to maintain a handle on reality by way of an elaborate method of timekeeping. It was calming to look back at what John and I were doing one year ago, and keep track of the days that way. It is just me, standing on the edge of a moment I never thought would arrive, tethered to someone who no longer exists in the present tense.Time has turned traitorous, reshaping vivid recollections into something blurred, soft-edged, mudgy. I want the sharpness back—the sound of his voice calling my name, the exact tilt of his head when he laughed—but instead I am left with echoes that refuse to hold their shape. This is the life left, the one that does not wait.

written_by_Harry.Original: Wendy risked another glance over her shoulder. Jack was on the sixth riser, clinging to the banister much as she was doing herself. He was still grinning, and dark blood oozed slowly through the grin and slipped down the line of his jaw. He bared his teeth at her.“I’m going to bash your brains in. Bash them right to fuck in.” He struggled up another riser.Panic spurred her, and the ache in her side diminished a little. She pulled herself up as fast as she could regardless of the pain, yanking convulsively at the banister. She reached the top and threw a glance behind her.He seemed to be gaining strength rather than losing it. He was only four risers from the top, measuring the distance with the roque mallet in his left hand as he pulled himself up with his right.“Right behind you,” he panted through his bloody grin, as if reading her mind. “Right behind you now, bitch. With your medicine.” She fled stumblingly down the main corridor, hands pressed to her side.The door to one of the rooms jerked open and a man with a green ghoulmask on popped out. “Great party, isn’t it?” he screamed into her face, and pulled the waxed string of a party favor. There was an echoing bang and suddenly crepe streamers were drifting all around her. The man in the ghoulmask cackled and slammed back into his room. She fell forward onto the carpet, full-length. Her right side seemed to explode with pain, and she fought off the blackness of unconsciousness desperately. Dimly she could hear the elevator running again, and beneath her splayed fingers she could see that the carpet pattern appeared to move, swaying and twining sinuously.The mallet slammed down behind her and she threw herself forward, sobbing. Over her shoulder she saw Jack stumble forward, overbalance, and bring the mallet down just before he crashed to the carpet, expelling a bright splash of blood onto the nap.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt1: Wendy could barely breathe as she ran up the old, creaking staircase, Jack close behind. “I’m gonna cave your head in, Wendy!” he screamed gleefully up at her, swinging his roque mallet back and forth in the air. Blood oozed out of his grinning mouth and down his chin. He looked like a real maniac, some deranged and bloodthirsty maniac. That gave Wendy the push she needed to block out her pain and pick up her pace. As she reached the next floor and darted through a connected corridor, a door suddenly swung open. A man emerged. He wore a rubbery and ghoulish green mask that seemed to be part of a Halloween costume. “Sing, dance, come celebrate! The party’s just starting!” he shouted, voice booming like a thunderstorm, and pulled the string on a party popper. A crack like lightning. The startling party favor spit confetti into the hallway, and Wendy gasped. The man slammed the door, vanishing back into the room. For a moment Wendy felt ridiculous, as if this whole thing were staged and harmless, like a haunted house attraction at an amusement park. But her body’s brief relaxation brought back her pain, which burst through her side. She crumpled in agony to the floor, vision blurring, battling to keep herself conscious; the carpet moved under her fingers. She heard the elevator rumble again, and knew that Jack had caught up. “There she is! Smile for me!” He lunged at her, narrowly missing her head with his mallet. Too much momentum. He lost his balance and crashed to the floor beside her with a thud. Blood spraying out of his mouth and onto the carpet as his cheek hit the ground. His eyes stayed closed. Wendy’s heart skipped a beat and for a moment she thought it was over. Then Jack opened one eye, almost playfully, and reached for her. She crawled forward, pushing herself back up and into a gradual sprint but Jack’s heavy footfalls trailed not far behind.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath came in ragged gasps, the sharp pain in her side like a splintered knife twisting deeper with each step. Jack’s laughter echoed up the staircase, a sound that was both guttural and gleeful, like a hyena that had found its prey. His mallet thudded against the bannister, a syncopated rhythm to the rising panic in her chest. She clawed at the handrail, her legs burning, her mind screaming for her body to keep moving.The corridor at the top of the stairs stretched out like a warped funhouse hallway. Shadows wavered on the walls, flickering with the uneven glow of the overhead bulbs. Wendy’s vision blurred, the carpet beneath her feet seeming to ripple like water. She stumbled but didn’t fall, her hand brushing the wall for balance as she pushed forward. A door burst open on her left, and a man in a green ghoul mask leapt out, his arms wide in mock celebration. “Party time!” he bellowed, the sound shrill and manic, accompanied by the wheezy squeal of a party favor. Wendy recoiled, her scream caught in her throat, as the ghoul slammed the door shut behind him, the sound echoing like a judge’s gavel.Jack’s voice boomed behind her, slurring threats that mixed rage with twisted humor. “Here’s Johnny!” The mallet whooshed through the air, missing her by inches as she collapsed against the wall. Her fingers dug into the carpet, her nails scraping the fibers, as the texture seemed to undulate beneath her touch. The elevator chimed in the distance, and her stomach turned as she realized he’d found another way up. Jack lunged forward, his momentum carrying him past her, and he hit the floor with a wet thud. Blood pooled beneath his face, staining the carpet in a grotesque bloom of crimson. Wendy blinked, the world tilting, as she willed herself to rise. The monster was down, but not out. Her escape depended on seconds, and the clock was still ticking.
written_by_Harry.Reason: Stephen King writes in a very straightforward, clear way, mostly avoiding bombastic imagery, symbolism, metaphor, with lines like: "Jack was on the sixth riser, clinging to the banister much as she was doing herself. He was still grinning, and dark blood oozed slowly through the grin and slipped down the line of his jaw." Because of this, Excerpt 1 is superior to Excerpt 2. Excerpt 1 has strong, clear action sentences, like "The startling party favor spit confetti into the hallway, and Wendy gasped" and "He lost his balance and crashed to the floor beside her with a thud." Excerpt 2 is in some ways better written (clearer grammar, less repetition), but emulates King's style less clearly, with over-the-top sentences like "Jack’s laughter echoed up the staircase, a sound that was both guttural and gleeful, like a hyena that had found its prey" and "Wendy’s vision blurred, the carpet beneath her feet seeming to ripple like water."

written_by_Celeste.Original: Wendy risked another glance over her shoulder. Jack was on the sixth riser, clinging to the banister much as she was doing herself. He was still grinning, and dark blood oozed slowly through the grin and slipped down the line of his jaw. He bared his teeth at her.“I’m going to bash your brains in. Bash them right the fuck in.” He struggled up another riser.Panic spurred her, and the ache in her side diminished a little. She pulled herself up as fast as she could regardless of the pain, yanking convulsively at the banister. She reached the top and threw a glance behind her.He seemed to be gaining strength rather than losing it. He was only four risers from the top, measuring the distance with the roque mallet in his left hand as he pulled himself up with his right.“Right behind you,” he panted through his bloody grin, as if reading her mind. “Right behind you now, bitch. With your medicine.” She fled stumblingly down the main corridor, hands pressed to her side.The door to one of the rooms jerked open and a man with a green ghoulmask on popped out. “Great party, isn’t it?” he screamed into her face, and pulled the waxed string of a party favor. There was an echoing bang and suddenly crepe streamers were drifting all around her. The man in the ghoulmask cackled and slammed back into his room. She fell forward onto the carpet, full-length. Her right side seemed to explode with pain, and she fought off the blackness of unconsciousness desperately. Dimly she could hear the elevator running again, and beneath her splayed fingers she could see that the carpet pattern appeared to move, swaying and twining sinuously.The mallet slammed down behind her and she threw herself forward, sobbing. Over her shoulder she saw Jack stumble forward, overbalance, and bring the mallet down just before he crashed to the carpet, expelling a bright splash of blood onto the nap.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: The pain exploded in Wendy's side like a grenade of glass shards as she clawed her way up the stairs, each step a new universe of agony. Behind her—too close, Christ, too close—came the whisper-thump of Jack's feet, a sound she'd once found comforting during their late-night kitchen raids but now sent ice-water terror coursing through her veins. His laughter floated up, thick and wet with blood, a madman's carousel music. "Honey, come back! I just want to bash your brains in!" The roque mallet whooshed through the air, stirring her hair like a lover's caress. She reached the top landing, lungs burning, heart thundering against her ribs like it wanted to escape her chest—and why shouldn't it? Getting away seemed like the only sane response to this nightmare. That's when the door to her left burst open and a figure lurched out, wearing a moldering green ghoul mask that might've been funny at some teenage Halloween party twenty years ago. "GREAT PARTY, ISN'T IT?" it screamed, blowing a party favor that unrolled with a wet, obscene sound. Then it was gone, door slamming with such force it shook dust from the ceiling. Wendy's legs betrayed her and she went down hard, the carpet beneath her fingers writhing like living things—thousands of insects fleeing from the violence above. The elevator hummed to life somewhere in the bowels of the hotel, its ancient gears grinding like arthritic teeth. She tried to push herself up, but her side shrieked in protest. Jack's shadow loomed over her, distorted and massive on the wall. The mallet swung down in a silver arc of death, missing her by inches as Jack stumbled, his momentum carrying him forward. He crashed face-first into the carpet, blood spraying from his mouth in a fine crimson mist. But Wendy knew he wouldn't stay down long. In the Overlook Hotel, nothing stayed dead for long.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Wendy looked back and wished she hadn’t. Jack had a malevolent smile on his face, and blood dripped from his open mouth down his chin like fruit juice. He swung a roque mallet steadily from side to side as he advanced up the staircase toward her. “C’mere, Wendy,” he said, “or I’ll paint this wall with your pretty, pink little brains.” Wendy turned back around and willed herself to keep going up the staircase. Her side was electric with pain, but she grit her teeth and kept going until she was in the corridor, where she broke into a run. She was almost at the end when a large figure jumped out in front of her. “You’ve gotta come to the party!” he shouted. He wore a green mask with hideously contorted plastic features. “Party favor?” he said, and jammed a little box toward her. She darted around him and continued down the hall, running faster this time. A door slammed violently behind her, and she turned to see that the man had disappeared.The pain in her side was becoming so severe that, when she took her next step forward, she collapsed under the agony of it. She tried to contain her scream, but it came roaring out of her anyway. She balled her hands into fists and pounded them into the carpet, which appeared to move beneath her, the patterns snakelike and fluid.The elevator made an ominous noise as it crept up the shaft, and she got on her knees, gripping the wall to try and stand. The elevator doors peeled open, revealing Jack with his heavy mallet. He spotted her and smiled. “Those pretty brains,” he said, and staggered in her direction. She began to run again, and he was behind her quickly. She felt the whoosh of the mallet, the air from its force grazing the back of her neck. She ducked away, and watched as Jack’s momentum sent him tumbling face-down onto the carpet, blood scattering like gory diamonds. She continued down the hall without looking back, her gasps so loud they blocked out all other sound.
written_by_Celeste.Reason: Excerpt 1 makes use of several techniques that departs from the original's style, while excerpt 2 seems tonally and stylistically on point. One of these departures, in excerpt 1, is the use of hyphenations like "whisper-thump" and "late-night" and "ice-water terror"; the original makes use of no such hyphenations (other than "full-length"). Excerpt 1 also uses more adorned language via similes than the original excerpt, such as "her fingers writhing like living things" and "The pain exploded in Wendy's side like a grenade of glass shards". In terms of similarities between the original and excerpt 2, there are several pieces of dialogue that feel adjacent to the original, such as "'C’mere, Wendy,' he said, 'or I’ll paint this wall with your pretty, pink little brains'" (p2) which feels close to, “'I’m going to bash your brains in. Bash them right the fuck in.'”

written_by_Lara_Wass.Excerpt1: Wendy gasped as she stumbled up the stairs, holding onto the railing with one hand. Each step sent a sharp pain through her side. She would’ve liked nothing better than to take a short rest but Jack’s voice behind her kept her going. “Wendy,” he slurred, grinning through bloody teeth, “come back here, sweetheart, so I can crush your bones like garlic cloves, what do you say?” She imagined feeling a gust of wind from the swing of Jack’s mallet behind her. At least the thundering of her pulse dulled the pain in her side. She turned corner after corner. Her feet barely touched the steps. The stairs seemed to stretch on endlessly. Finally, she reached the landing. She thought she had a second to breathe, when suddenly, a man—or something similar to a man— burst from a door. He wore a green ghoul mask and his suit reeked of mildew. Blowing a party favor that flapped in the air like a severed tongue, he shrieked, “Party time!” Wendy screamed and not knowing where else to go, stumbled backwards. The man vanished as abruptly as he’d appeared, slamming the door behind him. Wendy’s chest heaved. She collapsed to the floor. Her eyes felt heavy, but she told herself to stay awake, to just stay awake. Beneath her trembling fingers, the carpet seemed to writhe, its pattern shifting back and forth. She heard a ‘ding’ from the elevator. Jack’s footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder, but Jack’s momentum betrayed him as he crashed to the floor. Blood splattered in jagged streaks across the still shifting carpet. This was her moment. If not now, then when? Wendy got up, staggered, pain exploding in her side, and started running. Every step felt slow and heavy, as though she moved through quicksand. She imagined Jack rising behind her, unstoppable, coming closer by the second. She glanced back once, only once, before running headlong into the dark corridor.
written_by_Lara_Wass.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath hitched in her throat, a sob trapped in the cage of her ribs. Pain splintered through her side, a white-hot fire that threatened to consume her. But Jack was coming. She could hear his ragged breathing, the scrape of his workboots on the stairs, each footfall a hammer blow against her terror.He was grinning, she knew, a rictus of madness splitting his face, blood trickling from the corner of his mouth like a macabre smear of lipstick. The roque mallet, clutched in his fist, was an obscene promise of violence. “Wendy, my dear,” he’d croaked, the words thick with menace, “time for your medicine.”She scrambled to her feet, the pain a living thing in her side, a clawing beast that wanted to drag her down. But she couldn’t stop, not now. The corridor stretched before her, an endless tunnel of shadows and dread. A door flew open, and a man in a green ghoul mask lurched out, bellowing, “Party time!” He thrust a plastic horn at her, confetti raining down like grotesque snowflakes. Then he was gone, the door slamming shut behind him, leaving her in the echoing silence.The elevator whirred, the cables groaning like a tortured beast. Jack was still coming. She stumbled, her legs leaden, the carpet a treacherous bog beneath her feet. He was close now, she could feel the heat of his rage, smell the stale beer on his breath. The mallet whistled through the air, a whisper of death that grazed her shoulder. He lurched forward, off balance, and crashed to the floor with a sickening thud. Blood bloomed on the carpet, a crimson flower against the sickly green.He lay there, a broken doll, the mallet clattering away like a discarded toy. A moment of respite, a stolen breath in the suffocating darkness. But the elevator was moving again, its gears grinding like the teeth of a hungry monster. He would be back. He would always be back.
written_by_Lara_Wass.Reason: P1 is more similar to the Original than P2. Both E1 and the Original have a writing style that is very action-heavy and visually focused, with simple language (P1: "She heard a ding from the elevator. Jack's footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder..." O: "Dimly she could hear the elevator running again, and beneath her splayed fingers she could see that the carpet pattern appeared to move...Over her shoulder she saw Jack stumble forward.") P2, in contrast, attempts much more figurative language and overly-ornate imagery ("The elevator whirred, the cables groaning like a tortured beast" and the (pretty horrible) expression: "...a rictus of madness splitting his face..."). E1 and the Original, however, trade in more common, borderline cliche images, that are nevertheless effective for this genre of writing (Horror), such as the "pain exploding" in Wendy's side.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Original: The first day I did not think it was funny. I didn’t think it was funny the third day either, but I managed to make a little joke about it. “The most unfair thing about this whole business,” I said, “is that I can’t even date.” Well, you had to be there, as they say, because when I put it down on paper it doesn’t sound funny. But what made it funny (trust me) is the word “date,” which when you say it out loud at the end of a sentence has a wonderful teenage quality, and since I am not a teenager (okay, I’m thirty-eight), and since the reason I was hardly in a position to date on first learning that my second husband had taken a lover was that I was seven months pregnant, I got a laugh on it, though for all I know my group was only laughing because they were trying to cheer me up. I needed cheering up. I was in New York, staying in my father’s apartment, I was crying most of the time, and every time I stopped crying I had to look at my father’s incredibly depressing walnut furniture and slate-gray lamps, which made me start crying again.I had gotten on the shuttle to New York a few hours after discovering the affair, which I learned about from a really disgusting inscription to my husband in a book of children’s songs she had given him. Children’s songs. “Now you can sing these songs to Sam” was part of the disgusting inscription, and I can’t begin to tell you how it sent me up the wall, the idea of my two-year-old child, my baby, involved in some dopey inscriptive way in this affair between my husband, a fairly short person, and Thelma Rice, a fairly tall person with a neck as long as an arm and a nose as long as a thumb and you should see her legs, never mind her feet, which are sort of splayed.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.

Children’s songs. “Now you can sing these songs to Sam” was part of the disgusting inscription, and I can’t begin to tell you how it sent me up the wall, the idea of my two-year-old child, my baby, involved in some dopey inscriptive way in this affair between my husband, a fairly short person, and Thelma Rice, a fairly tall person with a neck as long as an arm and a nose as long as a thumb and you should see her legs, never mind her feet, which are sort of splayed.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.

written_by_Sophia.Original: There was a crime. But there were also the lovers. Lovers and their happy ends have been on my mind all night long. As into the sunset we sail. An unhappy inversion. It occurs to me that I have not traveled so very far after all, since I wrote my little play. Or rather, I’ve made a huge digression and doubled back to my starting place. It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The lingering image of Robbie and Cecilia, their figures receding down the driveway into the white mist, remains etched in my memory. It's a scene I've revisited countless times, a reminder of the love I shattered and the atonement I sought through my writing. In the twilight of my life, I question the nature of truth. Is a merciful fabrication, a crafted illusion of happiness, a greater kindness than the stark reality of a love tragically cut short? Robbie likely succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes. Cecilia perished in Balham Underground station during a bombing raid. Their letters lie preserved in a war museum, a testament to a love forever unfulfilled. Yet, in my final act of creation, I dared to defy fate. I granted them a reprieve, a fictional sanctuary where their love survived. It was a rebellion against the relentless march of time and tragedy. As the shadows lengthen, I wonder if I was right to weave this tapestry of hope. Would they have preferred the stark truth, the bitter knowledge of their unfulfilled love? Or is it a greater kindness to let them live on in my fictional world, forever young, forever in love? The question lingers, unresolved, like an echo in my mind. Perhaps there is no right answer to this age-old dilemma. Perhaps the truth, like beauty, lies in the eye of the beholder. A hopeful ending, even if untrue, is a more fitting tribute to their love than the harsh reality of their tragic fate.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.

It understands the tone better and keeps the focus on that central tension between truth and mercy. The original asks: “Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?” Option 2 echoes this clearly: “Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness?” Option 1 feels too written; it leans into metaphor and flourish – “Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript,” “love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent” – in a way that makes it feel less honest, less like the original’s clear, reflective sadness.

But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? At the edge of her fading strength, she allowed herself the faintest smile, perhaps at last, a merciful fiction was the highest form of kindness.
written_by_Rachael.Reason: Excerpt 1 is written in the same point-of-view as the original, and overall more closely mimics its style. Excerpt 2 is more descriptive and image-heavy than the original, while Excerpt 1's prose is leaner and more straightforward. Excerpt 2's use of third-person creates a barrier of distance between the reader and the situation, whereas Excerpt 1 directly addresses the reader---a quality it shares with the original.

written_by_Devin.Original: Then I called Reva. She answered on the fourth ring, panting and tense."I’m at the gym," she said. "Can we talk later?" We never did.On September 11, I went out and bought a new TV/VCR at Best Buy so I could record the news coverage of the planes crashing into the Twin Towers. Trevor was on a honeymoon in Barbados, I'd later learn, but Reva was lost. Reva was gone. I watched the videotape over and over to soothe myself that day. And I continue to watch it, usually on a lonely afternoon, or any other time I doubt that life is worth living, or when I need courage, or when I am bored. Each time I see the woman leap off the seventy-eighth floor of the North Tower—one high-heeled shoe slipping off and hovering up over her, the other stuck on her foot as though it were too small, her blouse untucked, hair flailing, limbs stiff as she plummets down, one arm raised, like a dive into a summer lake—I am overcome by awe, not because she looks like Reva, and I think it's her, almost exactly her, and not because Reva and I had been friends, or because I'll never see her again, but because she is beautiful. There she is, a human being, diving into the unknown, and she is wide awake.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: I stared at the television screen, the pixelated image of the Twin Towers collapsing, a grotesque loop of destruction playing over and over.  Reva, my dear Reva, was lost in the chaos, her voice a distant echo on the other end of a dropped phone call."Are you there?" I had asked, the dial tone buzzing in my ear.Hours earlier, the news had crackled to life, the blue glow of the television illuminating the room.  Trevor was away in Barbados, his honeymoon a cruel irony in the face of the unfolding tragedy.  I watched the towers crumble, the smoke billowing, a woman leaping from the inferno, her body a fragile arc against the backdrop of the burning sky. "She looks like Reva," I whispered, a strange sense of admiration washing over me.The woman's beauty, even in the face of death, was mesmerizing. Her courage, her desperation, her final act of defiance against the inevitable.I watched her fall, the image burned into my mind, a haunting reminder of the fragility of life.Reva, my wild, untamed friend, was gone, swallowed by the chaos, her laughter and vibrancy extinguished.  I mourned her loss, the emptiness a gaping hole in my soul.Days turned into weeks, the world a blur of muted colors and hollow sounds.  I watched the footage repeatedly, the woman's fall a morbid fascination, a symbol of our collective mortality.  In her final act, I saw a reflection of my own struggles, my own search for meaning in a world that often felt meaningless.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.

We never did." Excerpt 2 is closer to the original in this way, with straightforward lines like "She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym" and "Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good." written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: I'd stared at my cheap TV/VCR combo for hours that day, recording endless footage while sprawled on my beige couch, still warm from my body's perpetual indent. Trevor was in Barbados with his new wife, probably slathering on coconut-scented sunscreen while I watched people jump from burning buildings. I watched her fall hundreds of times, memorizing the way her skirt billowed, how her arms stretched wide as if embracing the sky. She became my obsession, this falling angel in sensible office wear. written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: I stood in the dim light of my living room, the boxed TV/VCR perched on the coffee table, its plastic wrapping still intact, a strange relic of the morning. I’d bought it not because I needed it, but because the weight of a new object felt like an anchor. Something solid. I could have told her to stay on the line, begged her to come over, but I didn’t. Later, I’d sit on the floor, knees pulled to my chest, watching footage of a woman leaping from the North Tower. Her dress caught the wind like a parachute, her body poised, graceful, falling as though she’d chosen to fly instead of burn. The likeness to Reva—her height, her hair—was undeniable, but I didn’t cry. I pressed pause, rewound, played it again, squinting at the screen, wondering if courage could be beautiful or if beauty was just what we saw in things we didn’t understand. Reva was gone. Lost. And yet, in that leap, she was eternal.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.

written_by_Sara.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.
written_by_Sara.Excerpt1: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.
written_by_Sara.Excerpt2: The night air, maybe tinged with the scent of some flowering tree I can’t identify, swirls through the gaps in the fencing.  The thrill elicited by this view—the tiny illuminated windows, the way human-scale elements are visibly enmeshed with the inhuman scale of the skyline—is something I associate with urban spaces.  The Hudson River, the Palisades on the other side, even the movement of the clouds, fail to trigger the same response.I breathe deeply, trying to identify the chemical compounds in the air.  I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed.  A yet-to-exist “we” glimpsed in the bundled debt, the traces of antidepressants in the water supply, the elaborate traffic system, the weather patterns.  I resolve to become the kind of artist who can transform bad forms of collectivity—bedbugs, or the crowds now surging toward Times Square—into glimpses of their potential for a kind of unity, a communal body.    And then there’s Noor, around whom the fiction of the world reorganizes itself.  I’m always trying to get back to her, but she’s never fully available, and this unavailability is central to her function.  She’s here, but only in the form of a promise I’ve made to myself to get up early and run the loop of the park, a promise I’ve already broken.I’m trying to think my way into a future state, but I’m too aware of my body on the bench to achieve the desired self-alienation.  I feel the pressure of the chain-link fence against my back, the bandanna flattening my hair.  I’m eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice running down my chin.  I’m having a mild lacrimal event, quietly tearing up.I’m never fully identical with myself.  There’s always a part of me that’s alien to me.  And this is where the hope, the utopian glimmer, resides—in the self-estrangement that enables me to imagine the past and present merging into something reinterpreted, whole.

written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
