Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_Hank.Reason: Lerner's style is poetic and, at times, overwritten, with strange and complex images like "the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc" and "a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body." Excerpt 1 imitates these stylistic quirks more closely, with images like "the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read." Meanwhile, Excerpt 2, while flowery and descriptive, is more straightforward, with images like "he buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine"

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_Celeste.Reason: Excerpt2 is closer to the original excerpt. Where paragraph1 is more explicit in its analogies ("The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses") and its judgements of those analogies ("The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity"), the original shows this judgement through tone rather than explicit argument. Excerpt2 maintains a greater neutrality in its depiction of its scene, and, like the original, allows this showing to reflect a judgement rather than specifically making an argument one way or another. This is shown well in contrasting the endings: the argument of paragraph1 ("I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.") compared to the unresolved image of paragraph2 ("My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.").

It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.

Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

written_by_James_Cato.Original: The Swede. During the war years, when I was still a grade school boy, this was a magical name in our Newark neighborhood, even to adults just a generation removed from the city's old Prince Street ghetto and not yet so flawlessly Americanized as to be bowled over by the prowess of a high school athlete. The name was magical; so was the anomalous face. Of the few fair-complexioned Jewish students in our preponderantly Jewish public high school, none possessed anything remotely like the steep-jawed, insentient Viking mask of this blue-eyed blond born into our tribe as Seymour Irving Levov.The Swede starred as end in football, center in basketball, and first baseman in baseball. Only the basketball team was ever any good—twice winning the city championship while he was its leading scorer—but as long as the Swede excelled, the fate of our sports teams didn't matter much to a student body whose elders, largely undereducated and overburdened, venerated academic achievement above all else. Physical aggression, even camouflaged by athletic uniforms and official rules and intended to do no harm to Jews, was not a traditional source of pleasure in our community—advanced degrees were. Nonetheless, through the Swede, the neighborhood entered into a fantasy about itself and about the world, the fantasy of sports fans everywhere: almost like Gentiles (as they imagined Gentiles), our families could forget the way things actually work and make an athletic performance the repository of all their hopes. Primarily, they could forget the war.The elevation of Swede Levov into the household Apollo of the Weequahic Jews can best be explained, I think, by the war against the Germans and the Japanese and the fears that it fostered. With the Swede indomitable on the playing field, the meaningless surface of life provided a bizarre, delusionary kind of sustenance, the happy release into a Swedian innocence, for those who lived in dread of never seeing their sons or their brothers or their husbands again.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.

written_by_Celeste.Original: The Swede. During the war years, when I was still a grade school boy, this was a magical name in our Newark neighborhood, even to adults just a generation removed from the city's old Prince Street ghetto and not yet so flawlessly Americanized as to be bowled over by the prowess of a high school athlete. The name was magical; so was the anomalous face. Only the basketball team was ever any good—twice winning the city championship while he was its leading scorer—but as long as the Swede excelled, the fate of our sports teams didn't matter much to a student body whose elders, largely undereducated and overburdened, venerated academic achievement above all else. Nonetheless, through the Swede, the neighborhood entered into a fantasy about itself and about the world, the fantasy of sports fans everywhere: almost like Gentiles (as they imagined Gentiles), our families could forget the way things actually work and make an athletic performance the repository of all their hopes. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: I was a boy of World War II and a boy of Newark. The war was far away and beyond my understanding, but the dread and threat of it spilled across the ocean and flooded every home in my city. Lots of our men were off fighting, and lots of them would never come home. Rations of oil and sugar were dispensed through clenched fists. We spent many nights huddled around the radio and forgetting to breathe. It was a time of need, which is—according to the comic books—the perfect time for a hero to arrive. Newark’s wartime hero was a high school boy named Seymour Irving Levov, who we nicknamed “The Swede” because of his blond hair and blue eyes. He was a paragon of greatness in my neighborhood, and his athletic ability was the stuff of legend; regardless of the sport he played, he always clinched the win for his team. The Swede’s consistent excellence in football, basketball, and baseball gave my community something to rally for. Being Jewish, most of us tended to prioritize academic achievements over physical feats, but the Swede changed things. We’d turn up to his games with homemade banners and clumsily invented cheers, among them “S-W-E-D-E, get this team to victory!” Watching the force of his kick, the graceful arch of his throw, and the shattering power of his swing shrouded us in a feeling of awe that was rarely experienced outside of Temple. When the Swede was on the field or on the court, my whole neighborhood was in the palm of his hand. He had unwittingly become a symbol of invincibility, of innocence, of hope that the terrible war would leave us unscathed, passed over like we had smeared lamb blood on our doors. Looking back, I don’t know if our hero arrived or if our hero was created, but the Swede was more than willing to shoulder the burden.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. Who could have predicted that from our community of intellectuals and worriers, of boys who measured their worth by the heft of their Hebrew school books and the precision of their bar mitzvah portions, would emerge this specimen of Nordic perfection? The Swede, with his impossible blue eyes and hair the color of straw, who moved across the athletic field like some magnificent shiksa fantasy come to life, became our collective dream of transformation. Here was a Jewish boy who could smash through defensive lines on the football field with the force of a Gentile, who could arc a basketball through the hoop with gymnastic grace, who could swing a baseball bat as if it were his birthright rather than something we'd borrowed from the other America. And how we needed him then, needed to believe in this anomaly, this statistical impossibility of nature who happened to daven at our synagogue! While our mothers whispered anxiously about cousins in Europe and our fathers scanned casualty lists in the Newark News with trembling hands, The Swede was our ticket to invincibility, our pass into that other realm where Jewish boys didn't have to be smart because they were beautiful, didn't have to be crafty because they were strong. We projected onto him all our desperate hopes of acceptance, of transcendence – this boy who looked like he'd stepped out of a Nazi propaganda poster but wore a chai around his neck and could recite his Haftorah portion without a single mistake. The Swede was our temporary escape from who we were, from what we feared, from the relentless drumbeat of war news that threatened to drown out even the sound of our prayers.

Perfect setup - walk around all day, drop paper in boxes, nobody breathing down your neck about quotas or time cards. Second day in, I'm working this neighborhood of tired houses with paint peeling off like dead skin when I see her. Big woman, not the Hollywood type, more like a female wrestler gone soft. She was watering dead flowers, her dress pulled tight across her ass, and when she bent over I nearly dropped the whole damn bag. "You the new mailman?" she asked, straightening up. I nodded, handed her some circulars and bills. She told me her husband was stationed in Germany, hadn't touched her in 8 months. Christ, the way she said it made my balls ache. I had a woman at home but she was always bitching about the rent, about my drinking, about everything. This one just wanted company. "Come by tonight," she said, giving me her address. I showed up at 9, half-drunk on cheap wine. The house smelled like potpourri and desperation. We didn't waste time talking - she led me straight to the bedroom, peeling off that housedress like a snake shedding its skin. Hell, you didn't even have to try - they were so desperate they'd fuck anything in a uniform. Sometimes the best jobs are the ones that give you just enough money to drink and just enough time to fuck.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. She stood at the door like she’d been waiting for me all day. “Cold out,” she said, her breath heavy, warm, sweet and rotten at the same time. “Yeah,” I said, “but I don’t mind.” I minded, but I wasn’t about to tell her that. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. The place was warm, smelled like burned toast and old carpet. She poured me whiskey instead of coffee, and that was better. We moved from the kitchen to the couch to the bedroom like it was something we’d done before. A few days passed like that. But the thing about loneliness is, it doesn’t go away just because you put your hands on someone. Eventually, the whiskey bottle emptied, the room started feeling smaller, and her laugh turned into something I didn’t want to hear. The job was still there, but the excitement was gone. So I delivered the mail, took my paycheck, and let her find another man to fill the spaces her husband left behind. Being a mailman wasn’t bad. Good work if you like walking. Better work if you don’t mind a little company along the way.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Cheerfulness was not in the job description for "Christmas mail carrier," so every day I showed up and delivered the damned mail. It was fitting that I found out about the job from our local drunk. Five bottles in at nine in the a.m. and the guy was babbling about being an elf for the US postal system. I'd rather have been six sheets to the wind than selling my soul for employment. And yet, I found the work to be rather freeing. I got to swan around town all day, moseying up to people's houses and eyeing their letters before dropping them off, washing my hands of them until tomorrow. It was simple, easy.I met the big woman my second day on the job. When I say big, she was actually quite short, but her tits were so massive they came up to her chin. My kind of woman. Until she opened her mouth and gave me her sad sap story. Her husband was enlisted some place far away. I couldn't tell what possibility bothered her most—that he was blowing guys' heads off or that he was getting blown. She went on and on about how it wasn't right for a married woman to be all alone. The big diamond ring was apparently a cure-all. This was news to me. I had a lady, myself, but I was lonely with her.After our shift, when the big woman invited me to come over later that night, I thought, to hell with being lonely ever again! written_by_Rachael.Reason: I think these two are close but I choose P1. written_by_Rachael.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. The one I keep here is fully paid-up green bow-tie-wearing fundamentalist terrorist. I sometimes wonder why I bother," said Samad bitterly, betraying the English inflections of twenty years in the country, "I really do. These days, it feels to me like you make a devil’s pact when you walk into this country. You hand over your passport at the check-in, you get stamped, you want to make a little money, get yourself started. but you mean to go back! Who would want to stay? Cold, wet, miserable; terrible food, dreadful newspapers — who would want to stay? In a place where you are never welcomed, only tolerated. Just tolerated. Like you are an animal finally house-trained. Who would want to stay? But you have made a devil’s pact... it drags you in and suddenly you are unsuitable to return, your children are unrecognizable, you belong nowhere." "Oh, that’s not true, surely." "And then you begin to give up the very idea of belonging. Suddenly this thing, this belonging, it seems like some long, dirty lie... and I begin to believe that birthplaces are accidents, that everything is an accident. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"

He tells his mother he wants to wear those ridiculous wigs and practice law. My other son, a fundamental terrorist! I just don't understand it, you raise your children the best you can, but they still grow into strangers."Irie said tentatively, "Oh, that's not true, surely."The disembodied loneliness of the past 20 years collapsed in on Samad as he thought about the state of his family, the state of himself."It's this place. I know it. You come here for all the right and righteous reasons. You don't mean to stay, not forever, but this place, it traps you. It's cold and wet here, and no one knows how to love, but you stay because things are working. By the time you realize you've made a mistake, you've been stained," Samad said. He looked at Irie, desperate to get the words out. "You can never fully be here, be English, because you're from someplace else, but you can never go back there, either! I know I can't. I'm tainted from my time here. I can never go home. I'm from nowhere now, and I'm going nowhere."

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Samad leaned back, fingers tightening around the stem of his glass, watching the amber liquid swirl, gathering his thoughts like a man recalling a half-forgotten dream. "You know, Irie, I did not come here to stay," he began, with the kind of dramatic pause he enjoyed, as if delivering some great revelation. "No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.

written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.

I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. written_by_Stefan.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. The one I keep here is fully paid-up green bow-tie-wearing fundamentalist terrorist. I sometimes wonder why I bother," said Samad bitterly, betraying the English inflections of twenty years in the country, "I really do. These days, it feels to me like you make a devil’s pact when you walk into this country. You hand over your passport at the check-in, you get stamped, you want to make a little money, get yourself started. but you mean to go back! Who would want to stay? Cold, wet, miserable; terrible food, dreadful newspapers — who would want to stay? In a place where you are never welcomed, only tolerated. Just tolerated. Like you are an animal finally house-trained. Who would want to stay? But you have made a devil’s pact... it drags you in and suddenly you are unsuitable to return, your children are unrecognizable, you belong nowhere." "Oh, that’s not true, surely." "And then you begin to give up the very idea of belonging. Suddenly this thing, this belonging, it seems like some long, dirty lie... and I begin to believe that birthplaces are accidents, that everything is an accident. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.

written_by_Benjamin.Original: Thomas Wolfe warned in the title of America’s great novel that “You Can’t Go Home Again.” I enjoyed the book but I never agreed with the title. I believe that one can never leave home. I believe that one carries the shadows, the dreams, the fears and dragons of home under one’s skin, at the extreme corners of ones eyes and possibly in the gristle of the ear lobe.Home is that youthful region where a child is the only real living inhabitant. Parents, siblings, and neighbors, are mysterious apparitions, who come, go, and do strange unfathomable things in and around the child, the region’s only enfranchised citizen.Geography, as such, has little meaning to the child observer. If one grows up in the Southwest, the desert and open skies are natural. New York, with the elevators and subway rumble and millions of people, and Southeast Florida with its palm trees and sun and beaches are to the children of those regions the way the outer world is, has been, and will always be. Since the child cannot control that environment, she has to find her own place, a region where only she lives and no one else can enter.I am convinced that most people do not grow up. We find parking spaces and honor our credit cards. We marry and dare to have children and call that growing up. I think what we do is mostly grow old. We carry accumulation of years in our bodies and on our faces, but generally our real selves, the children inside, are still innocent and shy as magnolias.We may act sophisticated and worldly but I believe we feel safest when we go inside ourselves and find home, a place where we belong and maybe the only place we really do.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.
written_by_Benjamin.Reason: While both paragraphs show connection to the original excerpt, Excerpt 1 is more closely oriented to the original in terms of voice and style. It carries over some of the sentimentality from the original in the very first sentence ("Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul."), while excerpt 2 takes a different, more personal, and more memoiristic approach ("I imagined him taller than he should have been"). While both paragraphs mention that people never leave home, never really grow up (and bring in the dragons and parking spots!), excerpt 1 stays more firmly within the confines of the lyrical, melancholic reflection while excerpt 2's tone is more explanatory, and incorporates an ode to childhood more generally.

written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.
written_by_Cara.Reason: In terms of narrative style, Excerpt 2 is more aligned with the original excerpt. While Excerpt 1 is largely in the second person, Excerpt 2's use of first person (both plural and singular) is consistent with the original POV. Excerpt 2's voice also bears more similarity to the original, particularly the sentence about home being "a place of shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons." While Excerpt 1's sentence on the same subject matter is quite short, Excerpt 2 captures the flowing, descriptive quality of the original.

written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: When Thomas Wolfe declared you can't go home again, he hadn't reckoned with the stubborn geography of the heart, that relentless compass that forever points to our beginning place. Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.
written_by_Stefan.Reason: Neither of these seem particularly stylistically close to the original, but I would choose E2 between the two. This type of sentence isn’t really present in the original. In the original, the authorial presence is made very clear by the presence of many “I” statements – “I enjoyed” “I believe” “I am convinced” “I think”. These are totally absent from P1, but they are at least used once in P2: “ I've watched children”. written_by_Benjamin.Original: That night at the hotel, in our room with the long empty hall outside and our shoes outside the door, a thick carpet on the floor of the room, outside the windows the rain falling and in the room light and pleasant and cheerful, then the light out and it exciting with smooth sheets and the bed comfortable, feeling that we had come home, feeling no longer alone, waking in the night to find the other one there, and not gone away; all other things were unreal. We slept when we were tired and if we woke the other one woke too so one was not alone. Often a man wishes to be alone and a girl wishes to be alone too and if they love each other they are jealous of that in each other, but I can truly say we never felt that. We could feel alone when we were together, alone against the others. It has only happened to me like that once. I have been alone while I was with many girls and that is the way that you can be most lonely. But we were never lonely and never afraid when we were together.I know that the night is not the same as the day: that all things are different, that the things of the night cannot be explained in the day, because they do not then exist, and the night can be a dreadful time for lonely people once their loneliness has started. But with Catherine there was almost no difference in the night except that it was an even better time. If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: The hotel balcony looked out through the rain down to the riviera. The houses outside were gray. In the dark we listened to the rain on the roof, and Catherine turned to me to say nothing, and we lay like that for a while. The slope of her shoulder was like a mountain. It could have always been there like a mountain in the distance, and I could have not known I'd memorized it. Then she spoke. "Do you need me tomorrow?""Shush. Shush," I said. I didn't like that I had to say it. It was that knowledge of what not to say that filled more in me than any words could. She turned away. The rain hit thick on the balcony tiles. The sheets felt soft. I wanted her to focus on that. The sheets, the small room, the wind blowing the rain sideways. We didn't burn the lights and let the moon through the thin curtain show. In similar rooms and nights like these, I had felt the worst of them alone. What I didn't know I needed was that same stifled quiet, the same rain, the same room. Perhaps I expected less of me to fill it all. I felt at home when I felt her most and heard her least. With the crowded taverns, I'd go and sit between stone shoulders and feel no need of my being there. What made her mine was what she never asked of me."Maybe tomorrow," I said. She said nothing. The rain whipped on. Soon, the streets outside would be muddy and thick. The mud would cake our shoes. The ground at its meanest like that. It takes us at its softest. The ground breaks everyone it breaks itself for. All men, the very good and the very gentle and the very brave, all go quiet in the ground. It clings and cakes to you. Yet you can pull. Yet you can crawl and drag onto more mud, more breaking, more ground that will eventually take you."Maybe tomorrow you come with me," I still said to the rain.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: The rain was a constant companion that night, its soft patter against the window a soothing melody. I lay in bed, the sheets a cool caress against my skin, and felt a warmth bloom within me. It was a warmth that had nothing to do with the fire crackling in the hearth, but rather with the presence beside me. Catherine. My Catherine. With her there, I felt a sense of belonging, a feeling of completeness that I had never experienced before.We had always possessed this uncanny ability, Catherine and I, to be utterly alone, yet entirely together.  In the past, I had often found myself adrift in a sea of faces, surrounded by people, yet feeling utterly isolated.  But with Catherine, it was as if we created our own world, a world where words were unnecessary, where our thoughts flowed together like two streams merging into one. written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I lay in the hotel bed with Catherine, listening to the rain beat against the windows, and I felt good. Really good. The sheets were cool and smooth, and Catherine's breathing was soft and even beside me, and for the first time in a long while I wasn't alone. Not the way you can be alone in a crowded café or alone in someone else's bed, but really not alone. We didn't need to talk. That was the fine thing about Catherine. You could be quiet with her and it felt right. The rain kept coming down outside and the street lamps made yellow pools on the wet pavement below, and I watched them and felt Catherine's warmth against me, solid and real. I had been with other women before, plenty of them, but it was always like being alone, even when you were holding them. With Catherine it was different. She knew about being alone too, and maybe that's why we could be alone together without it hurting. The world breaks everyone sooner or later, that's what I'd learned. It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. But Catherine and I, we were already broken when we found each other, so maybe that's why we fit. We didn't need to pretend. The rain was coming down harder now, drumming against the roof, and Catherine stirred beside me but didn't wake. I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true. But for now we had this - the rain outside and the warm bed and the knowledge that we weren't alone. Sometimes that's all you get in this world, these small moments of peace before the breaking starts again. But maybe if you're lucky, you find someone who knows how to pick up the pieces with you. Catherine knew about pieces. She knew about breaking. And here in this room, with the rain coming down, we had put our broken pieces together and made something whole.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: We looked around the hotel room when we opened the door. To be away together! Catherine’s arm looped around my shoulders with mine around her waist. She’d been clearer to me than myself, because I didn’t spend all day studying myself the way I spent all day studying her. My investigation was not complete. We made drinks and sat in the corner chairs. It didn’t matter much that we hadn’t been in the room before. A sense of being at home, of familiarity, accompanied me with Catherine wherever we went together. Rain came down outside in long slants and we listened to the sound in between our conversations and during our sips of drink. The glasses emptied and we filled them up. We could sit in silence, alone with our thoughts but connected somehow. There was the pleasure of watching another think without fear of being caught. She might have even had the expectation of me watching her think. With others long moments of silence had an itchy quality. With friends and lovers I had clawed back into conversation when it faltered or ended naturally. This time as we lay in bed gazing around at the room my mind wandered to those distant relationships and those people who hadn’t met someone like Catherine. Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited. I reached out and touched her skin and watched my finger trace a white line down her shoulder. A melancholy settled over me. The nature of the world when taken without this comfort breaks everyone and kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. Perhaps those who suffer this fate can persevere for a time or recover from its cruelty in short bursts. Still, suffer they will. When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.
