To be away together!" and "My investigation was not complete." The voice of the original is almost naive, and the rhythms are simple, repetitive: "But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry." The second excerpt's voice is much more sophisticated and descriptive: "Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited." The simple phrasing is better mimicked in the first excerpt, which repeats the verb "break," as the original does: "It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. ... I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true."

written_by_Connor.Original: That night at the hotel, in our room with the long empty hall outside and our shoes outside the door, a thick carpet on the floor of the room, outside the windows the rain falling and in the room light and pleasant and cheerful, then the light out and it exciting with smooth sheets and the bed comfortable, feeling that we had come home, feeling no longer alone, waking in the night to find the other one there, and not gone away; all other things were unreal. We slept when we were tired and if we woke the other one woke too so one was not alone. Often a man wishes to be alone and a girl wishes to be alone too and if they love each other they are jealous of that in each other, but I can truly say we never felt that. We could feel alone when we were together, alone against the others. It has only happened to me like that once. I have been alone while I was with many girls and that is the way that you can be most lonely. But we were never lonely and never afraid when we were together.I know that the night is not the same as the day: that all things are different, that the things of the night cannot be explained in the day, because they do not then exist, and the night can be a dreadful time for lonely people once their loneliness has started. But with Catherine there was almost no difference in the night except that it was an even better time. If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt1: The rain came hard against the window, steady and thin, running down in lines like wire. The room was warm, the sheets smooth beneath my hand. Catherine lay beside me, her breathing even, her body curved just enough toward mine. I could hear the water in the street below, the hush of tires passing, the occasional step of someone hurrying through the wet. It was a good sound. It made the room feel safer. I turned my head and looked at her. Her hair was against her cheek, and I wanted to brush it away, but I didn’t. There was time for that. There was time for everything now, and it felt like all the time in the world.She stirred but did not wake. I watched her for a while. I had been alone before. I had lain in beds in places that were not home, in cities where the streets ran like rivers and the lights burned cold and far away, and I had felt the loneliness of it even with someone there. But not with her. That was the difference. With her, even silence felt full. We could sit in it, breathe in it, and nothing would press between us. It was something rare, something I had not known before. I had known plenty of other things. The empty hours in cafés, the taste of bad brandy, the way a night could stretch and break you down. I had known the sound of laughter that didn’t belong to me, and the way people looked past you when they didn’t want to see. But this was different.Outside, the rain did not stop. It never did. The world went on breaking people, wearing them down like stone in a river, like wood left too long in the salt and the sun. It broke the best first, the gentle ones, the ones who carried too much in them. The others it let last longer, but not forever. No one lasted forever. But for now, for this moment, there was just the quiet, the warmth of the sheets, the softness of her breath, and the rain against the glass.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt2: I spent the night with Catherine in our hotel room overlooking the little square with the rain coming down outside, our bodies naked under the sheets, and the sheets were smooth cotton, and they were good sheets, and I told Catherine so, and she put her feet between my bare legs, and her feet were cold but soon they became warm, and I put my fingers between her hair, and it felt like we were at home together, and I told her so. She smiled and looked at the rain trickle down the glass of the window, and I knew I did not need to say anything else about that.  Because she understood, unlike so many others who I've sought to find and spend time with, who I thought understood and did not, and when I tried to be together with them, our togetherness was lonelier than our solitude. With Catherine, in our togetherness we were solitary still. We held each other up and made each other feel courage in mutual independence. She kissed my cheek, and I looked up at the light on the ceiling, which was turned off, but I could see the streetlights reflect into it through the window. Just the barest bit of light there in the glass, and I thought of how fragile it all was, because this is not a world for rareness. It is a harsh world which breaks everyone, especially the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. It rises to break them all the more, and the more bravery and goodness and gentleness it is met with, the more harshness it responds with. I put my hand on Catherine's shoulder, and I felt the warmth there, and I wondered whether warmth existed because of cold or cold because of warmth. If it was a cold world, as it was a harsh one, what it meant that our bodies were warm when we lived and cold when we died. I thought there was no way to stay warm forever. No matter how long we held each other, the cold still eventually came.
written_by_Connor.Reason: While I feel that both of these paragraphs are not too similar to the Original, as they are both a bit too imagistic, E1 is more similar than P2. This is primarily because E2 operates in a much more active, scenic space--the lovers touching each other, interacting with each other, descriptions of the room as it relates to their movements--where as E1 and the Original are more interior and introspective. Details are noticed, but most of the paragraph space is taken up with the narrator's musings and rememberings ("P1: I had been alone before. I had lain in beds in places that were not home..." O: "I have been alone while I was with many girls and that is the way that you can be the most lonely."). E1 also mirrors the more simple sentence structures and descriptions of the Original (P1: "It broke the best first, the gentle ones, the ones who carried too much in them" O: "The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places." vs. the more lyric E2 "If it was a cold world, as it was a harsh one, waht it meant that our bodies were warm when we lived and cold when we died.").

written_by_Cara.Original: One Saturday morning, the man who had actually killed the former premier went to his dead uncle’s garage, where he’d hidden the red car, started it up, then sat behind the wheel, thinking. Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier? Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. Afterward, he would climb up on the hood of his red car and, addressing the people, propose a new movement that would eschew violence and rule by justice and gentleness forever. Also firmness, of course. A merciful firmness the people would instantly respect.Or he could forget the whole thing, go back to being the man he’d been before the first killing: a frightened, passive nobody.This thought made him sicker than the thought of another round of screaming and crunching.He leaped out of the still running red car, threw the garage door open, and, feeling alive and decisive, stood blinking in the morning sunlight, readying himself for his task.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: He sat in Uncle Pete's cherry-red Civic (deceased), which smelled like those little pine trees times infinity, contemplating what the HR folks call Career Enhancement via Strategic Premier Elimination. The last one had been easier—younger him, dumber him, him before the Sleep-EZ pills and the nightly Personal Terror Management Sessions. Now he knew things. Like how a dying premier's eyes go all WhatThe? and BetYouFeelBadNow. Like how the headlines say Justice Served! while your brain screams MurderGuy! MurderGuy! at 3 A.M. But this new premier? Total sicko. Made the last one look like a Kindness Enhancement Specialist. The way those thick-necked guards stood around him at press conferences, all We'reNotThinkingAboutGunsUnderOurJackets. The way he signed those Special Citizen Reduction Orders with that gold pen, smirking. A guy could become somebody, taking him out. Could go on TV, start a movement: Area Man Admits to Double-Premier Elimination, Seeks Followers. Better than sitting here hyperventilating in Uncle Pete's garage, waiting for the next Premier-Initiated Civic Improvement Program to accidentally-on-purpose disappear more "undesirable elements." The old him, Pre-Premier-Removal him, would've just gone home, watched GameShows™. But that guy? That guy was dead as Uncle Pete. He grabbed the door handle, feeling that old familiar Here-We-Go-Again tingle. Time to make history. Again.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.
written_by_Cara.Reason: The Original paragraph is straightforward, slightly lyrical, and introspective, centering around the thought process of a man who has killed one premier and is considering killing another ("Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier?"). Excerpt 2 mirrors this style more closely, staying straightforward and linear in its portrayal of the man's thought process — and critically, staying in our world ("Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded?"). Excerpt 1, in stark contrast, introduces new elements of worldbuilding, differentiating itself from both Excerpt 2 and the Original in style and tone ("Better than sitting here hyperventilating in Uncle Pete's garage, waiting for the next Premier-Initiated Civic Improvement Program to accidentally-on-purpose disappear more "undesirable elements."") It is more novel and experimental in its style and tone than Excerpt 2 and the Original paragraph ("The way those thick-necked guards stood around him at press conferences, all We'reNotThinkingAboutGunsUnderOurJackets.").

The last one had been easier—younger him, dumber him, him before the Sleep-EZ pills and the nightly Personal Terror Management Sessions. Now he knew things. Like how a dying premier's eyes go all WhatThe? and BetYouFeelBadNow. Like how the headlines say Justice Served! while your brain screams MurderGuy! MurderGuy! at 3 A.M. But this new premier? Total sicko. Made the last one look like a Kindness Enhancement Specialist. The way those thick-necked guards stood around him at press conferences, all We'reNotThinkingAboutGunsUnderOurJackets. The way he signed those Special Citizen Reduction Orders with that gold pen, smirking. A guy could become somebody, taking him out. Could go on TV, start a movement: Area Man Admits to Double-Premier Elimination, Seeks Followers. Better than sitting here hyperventilating in Uncle Pete's garage, waiting for the next Premier-Initiated Civic Improvement Program to accidentally-on-purpose disappear more "undesirable elements." The old him, Pre-Premier-Removal him, would've just gone home, watched GameShows™. But that guy? That guy was dead as Uncle Pete. He grabbed the door handle, feeling that old familiar Here-We-Go-Again tingle. Time to make history. Again.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Original: One Saturday morning, the man who had actually killed the former premier went to his dead uncle’s garage, where he’d hidden the red car, started it up, then sat behind the wheel, thinking. Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier? Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: The red car was old, a wheezing relic. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? Murder wasn’t a thing you could just stop doing like sugar or carbs. It left its hooks in you, lodged under the ribs, twisting whenever you tried to breathe easy. The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. And for what? A better world? Please. The world had gone on, more evil, more absurd. The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it? To step into the role, a public avenger, claim the credit, lead the charge? But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one. That thought sickened him. No. Obscurity was the real death. He flung the door open, the cold air a slap. Time to go.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.

The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it?"). written_by_Mariah Kreutter.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.
written_by_Mariah Kreutter.Excerpt2: The man in the red car, a car he'd stashed in his dead uncle's garage, a car he sat in now, thinking, This is it.  It was a Saturday.  He was grappling.  With his conscience.  The premier had to go.  This premier, worse than the last.  And the last one, well, he'd taken care of that.  Hadn't he?  The man in the red car, the car in the dead uncle's garage, the man who'd done it before, the man grappling, the man with the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  He'd thought they'd be a good thing, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  A just price.  For taking out the bad guy.  But now he was thinking, Maybe not.  Maybe the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, maybe they weren't a just price.  Maybe they were just panic attacks, nightmares, cold sweats.  The man in the red car, the car in the garage, the dead uncle, the dead premier, the grappling, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, the thinking, the thinking, the thinking.  Go or stay.  This was it.  Or it wasn't.  Do it again and step into the light.  He could lead a movement.  Take credit.  Tell the world, You want justice? I'm justice.  Or go back to being the guy he'd been before.  The guy no one suspected.  The guy who did what he had to do and then went back to work on Monday.  Like nothing had happened.  The thought of it, the thought of going back to being that guy, that's what made him leap out of the car.

The man in the red car, the car in the garage, the dead uncle, the dead premier, the grappling, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, the thinking, the thinking, the thinking.” E1 leans on different stylistic elements than P2, such as the original author’s tendency to used exaggerated ‘official’ language to highlight its absurdity – “his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” Its sentence structure also more closely mirrors the original because it uses a mixture of short and long sentences rather than a series of extremely short sentences (as in P2).

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: In the heart of Charles de Gaulle Airport, where the Parisian winter raged outside, a vision of timeless beauty emerged amidst the sterile expanse of the terminal.  A striking woman, her skin kissed by the sun like ancient amber, her eyes pools of liquid obsidian, moved with the grace of a lioness through the bustling crowd.  A flowing, emerald-green kaftan draped her form, its edges embroidered with intricate symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations.  A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.

A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.

written_by_Devin.Original: She was beautiful and lithe, with soft skin the color of bread and eyes like green almonds, and she had straight black hair that reached to her shoulders, and an aura of antiquity that could just as well have been Indonesian as Andean. She was dressed with subtle taste: a lynx jacket, a raw silk blouse with very delicate flowers, natural linen trousers, and shoes with a narrow stripe the color of bougainvillea. ‘This is the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen,’ I thought, when I saw her pass by with the stealthy stride of a lioness, while I waited in the check-in line at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris for the plane to New York.She was a supernatural apparition who existed only for a moment and disappeared into the crowd in the terminal.It was nine in the morning. It had been snowing all night, and traffic was heavier than usual in the city streets, and even slower on the highway, where trailer trucks were lined up on the shoulder and automobiles steamed in the snow. Inside the airport terminal, however, it was still spring.I stood behind an old Dutch woman who spent almost an hour arguing about the weight of her eleven suitcases. I was beginning to feel bored when I saw the momentary apparition who left me breathless, and so I never knew how the dispute ended. Then the ticket clerk brought me down from the clouds with a reproach for my distraction. By way of an excuse, I asked her if she believed in love at first sight. "Of course," she said. "The other kinds are impossible."
written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.

"Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers.") Excerpt 1, like the original, is slightly more straightforward in its descriptions (ex. "Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake.").

written_by_Harry.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt1: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt2: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.
written_by_Harry.Reason: The Original paragraph is straightforward and nostalgic in tone ("I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up"). Excerpt 1 echoes this tone and style with its simplicity and exploration of loss and grief ("I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves.") — the tone and style are consistent. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, contains the same narrative but portrays it in a more heady, heavy-handed prose ("It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine."). Phrases like "amidst this desolation" would not fit in either Excerpt 1 or the Original paragraph, which are told in a more immediately human voice.

I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. According to a long and very unflattering story in the Times, Walter had made quite a mess of his professional life out there in the nation’s capital. His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: In the quiet confines of Ramsey Hill, the news of Walter Berglund's troubles, as trumpeted by the unforgiving clarion of The New York Times, seemed to echo in a vacuum, its resonance muffled by the simple fact that Walter and Patty had moved to Washington, D.C., two years prior.  It was as if the man portrayed in the article - arrogant, ethically compromised - was a stranger, a doppelganger bearing little resemblance to the Walter they thought they knew.  The Walter they remembered was the lone cyclist, a beacon of environmental idealism in a sea of gas-guzzling SUVs, not someone enmeshed in the murky depths of coal industry dealings.But life, like memory, is a fickle thing, prone to distortions and revisions.  The Berglunds, in their Ramsey Hill days, were pioneers of a sort, young urban homesteaders staking their claim in a neighborhood that had seen better days.  Their Victorian house, a relic of a bygone era, was a testament to their tireless efforts, a monument to sweat equity built amidst the blight of boarded-up windows and rampant vandalism.Patty, a former college athlete, stood out in this gritty landscape, a figure of unflinching resilience pushing her stroller through streets littered with broken glass and the detritus of urban decay.  She was a woman who could change a diaper with one hand while wielding a spackle knife with the other, a woman who could soothe a crying child while simultaneously warding off the advances of an aggressive panhandler.Her days fell into a familiar rhythm: the comforting drone of public radio, the midday reward of a zinfandel, the constant juggling act of motherhood and home renovation.  She was a woman straddling two worlds, one foot planted in the world of middle-class aspirations, the other in the harsh reality of her surroundings. And yet, beneath this veneer of normalcy, there was a hint of vulnerability, a flicker of something unfulfilled.  The Berglunds, for all their outward success, were a study in contrasts, a living embodiment of the American Dream's inherent contradictions.  They were remarkable and yet flawed, their idealism tempered by the compromises and disappointments of life.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: It must have been easier, in the late stages, not to have the story spilling directly into local news outlets. Easier to keep up the front. The Times erred only once, as far as one can tell, and described Walter as "arrogant" and "ethically compromised." Yet this dissonant portrait would not have resonated locally anyway, since Walter and Patty had already moved to Washington, D.C., about two years earlier. He'd gone to work for some energy-conservation organization after his youngest left college. It was hard to reconcile the full story with the optimistic, rural, green Walter who appeared to have been hampered and then corrupted by city life. Nowhere was the irony more poignant than back in St. Paul. The memory of the simple Walter, committed to punishing bad neighbors and raising good kids, stood in contrast to the fall of a man now willing to cut deals with big coal companies and ethically bend the rules in pursuit of his goals.To understand the derailment of Walter and Patty Berglund, one must remember those early years in Ramsey Hill when they were young pioneers in a neighborhood struggling to reclaim its nineteenth-century grandeur. The Berglunds bought their big Victorian for a song in 1990, when nobody wanted those properties because of broken windows, stray gunshots, and derelict urbanites holding out in rotting pillboxes. Walter and Patty invested time and sweat in their chosen project. They painted and fixed things, not merely as homeowners, but with the diligence of proselytizers converting neglected souls to middle-class potential. It was hard to miss Patty in those days—strolling down Laurel Avenue with a conspicuous brown stroller and her whipcord shoulders; she looked like the jock she claimed to be. She parked the shiny Subaru in sensible places and took the kids and cocker spaniel, Polly, to yoga classes and after-school programs out in the safer suburbs. Patty strengthened her household with Parks and Recreation and then afternoons of Wait Wait Don't Tell Me! followed by the zinfandel hour. At 10 p.m., after the kids were in bed, she was often seen stripping paint from woodwork or rehabbing furniture bought at local garage sales. She was benevolently juggling the old, the new, and the as-yet-unmade.

Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The irony of Walter's transformation from eco-warrior to coal industry collaborator wasn't lost on the former neighbors in Ramsey Hill, though they nursed their disappointment with the kind of passive-aggressive Midwestern restraint that had always made Patty want to scream into her wine glass. The Times piece had painted him as a sellout, which wasn't exactly wrong but missed the essentially Walter-ish quality of his failure – the way his very righteousness had somehow curdled into its opposite, like milk left too long in a virtuous organic glass bottle. In the early days, watching him pedal off to work on his secondhand Schwinn, his messenger bag stuffed with environmental impact reports and local-economy manifestos, the neighbors had seen him as a kind of secular saint, the sort of man who made them feel better about their own smaller gestures toward planetary salvation. Patty, meanwhile, had performed her own theatre of domestic virtue, pushing that double-wide stroller past crack houses and shuttered storefronts with the kind of aggressive cheer that suggested she was either oblivious to danger or actively courting it. The Victorian they'd bought for a song had been their shared project, their statement of faith in the possibility of redemption – not just of a house or a neighborhood, but of a whole way of life that was vanishing as surely as the ozone layer they worried about while listening to All Things Considered. Every stripped floorboard and replastered wall had seemed to say: See? This is how you do it. This is how you live righteously in a fallen world. But righteousness, it turned out, was a kind of intoxicant, and Walter had drunk deeper than most. The coal deal was just the logical endpoint of his conviction that he alone could save the world – a conviction that had grown more desperate and less discriminating as the world had shown itself increasingly resistant to being saved. The neighbors, sipping their own carefully sourced wine and tending their own carefully curated gardens, could afford to judge him now, secure in the knowledge that they, at least, had never tried quite so hard to be good.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_Sophia.Original: We could have it for a month, she told me over the phone. Not that I think I’ll need that much time.Would I ever get used to this kind of talk? Even as I wondered what to do about my mail—let it pile up, have the post office forward it or hold it for me—I found it unthinkable to ask how long I should plan to be gone.It’s not like I’ve picked a date, she said. Though, as I say, I am ready to go. You could even say I’m impatient to go, which comes partly from my having already given so much thought to dying but also from having reached the limits of what I think I can bear. But I don’t know what my body will do.Though she’d been feeling much better since she went off chemo, her symptoms could change from day to day, and the meds she was taking to suppress them had some side effects too.In any case, I want things to happen naturally, she said. I feel like I’ll know when it’s time.But you—well, you won’t know, she said. Obviously I won’t be making a big announcement. Like the coming of the Lord, she said jokingly: You will not know the day or hour.She had decided not to tell anyone about our plans. I’ve come this far, I don’t want to risk some stupid intervention, she said, or even a tiny disruption. I want peace.No one was to know where we were.And, for your own protection, she told me, you need to play dumb: I never told you what I was going to do, you weren’t even aware that I had the drug.I had, in fact, already told one other person everything, but I did not say this.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.

What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? written_by_Rachael.Original: No live organism can continue for long to exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality; even larks and katydids are supposed, by some, to dream. Hill House, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within; it had stood so for eighty years and might stand for eighty more. Within, walls continued upright, bricks met neatly, floors were firm, and doors were sensibly shut; silence lay steadily against the wood and stone of Hill House, and whatever walked there, walked alone. Dr John Montague was a doctor of philosophy; he had taken his degree in anthropology, feeling obscurely that in this field he might come closest to his true vocation, the analysis of supernatural manifestations. He was scrupulous about the use of his title because, his investigations being so utterly unscientific, he hoped to borrow an air of respectability, even scholarly authority, from his education. It had cost him a good deal, in money and pride, since he was not a begging man, to rent Hill House for three months, but he expected absolutely to be compensated for his pains by the sensation following upon the publication of his definitive work on the causes and effects of psychic disturbances in a house commonly known as ‘haunted.’ He had been looking for an honestly haunted house all his life. When he heard of Hill House he had been at first doubtful, then hopeful, then indefatigable; he was not the man to let go of Hill House once he had found it.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.  For eighty years it had borne silent witness to untold horrors, and eighty more it might endure, its walls upright, its floors firm, its doors closed, a tomb of secrets.  Within its depths, Dr. John Montague, a man of letters and a scholar of the unseen, sought to unravel the mysteries that clung to the house like cobwebs.  His excitement was a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed beneath his skin as he surveyed his conquest.He had come seeking a haunted house, and Hill House, with its malevolent reputation, seemed to fit the bill.  It had cost him dearly, this pursuit of the paranormal, both in the coin of the realm and the currency of his reputation.Yet, he was undeterred, his resolve as firm as the foundations of the house itself.  He would have his proof, his definitive study of psychic disturbances, a testament to the unseen world that whispered just beyond the veil of perception. Dr. Montague, a man who clung to his title as if it were a life raft in a sea of skepticism, was determined to conquer the mysteries of Hill House.  He would face the darkness, the unseen forces that lurked within, and emerge with the truth, or be consumed by the shadows that stretched long and hungry within the walls of the house.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. written_by_Molly.Excerpt1: Dr. John Montague stood before Hill House, a place that loomed as though waiting, its cold stones heavy with silence. As he crossed the threshold, the air seemed to shift, pressing lightly against his skin as though the house was tasting him. He paused, glancing back at the gravel drive that led away, the thought fleeting: nothing here would let him leave unmarked. The door shut behind him with a finality that echoed briefly, then faded, swallowed entirely by the unbroken, unnerving silence of Hill House.
written_by_Molly.Excerpt2: Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness. A house born within a garden of oleander, no person alive could claim witness to its birth, and so the poisonous intentions of the house were known only to itself. He believed himself, after conducting a lifelong search for a haunted home, to have found Hill House; this was a false belief. It was Hill House that found Dr. Montague, alone in his study, nursing his failures with cognac in hand as he lingered over a newspaper clipping which happened to mention, offhandedly, the strange occurrences of a mansion atop a hill in a small New England town. This home could contain answers, he thought, slowing his car to park beneath the ominous gaze of the house's front windows, answers only I can find.

written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: The Misfit looked at the old woman who had risen on to her knees in the damp grass and begun to pray. Hearing the familiar words made him lose his sense of urgency for it recalled to his mind the prayers he had memorized and repeated as a boy. The promise of redemption had appealed to him then but as a grown man he knew to trust only those things he could see for himself and verify firsthand. He would have given anything to have proof of his own everlasting soul or anyone else’s, but no sign had ever revealed itself to him and so the promises had turned curdled and turned bitter in his heart. The grandmother watched the Misfit’s face change as she prayed. She saw him illuminated and transformed into a young child, long before he was ever a killer, with a soul as pure and innocent as her son’s had once been. “You’re one of my own children!” she cried and reached out to him. But the sudden flicker of her outstretched white hand made the Misfit recoil and shoot. He shot three times in quick succession until she had crumpled and fallen back into the ditch. He stood over her in the ditch and watched her lips settle into a faint smile. He removed his wire-rimmed glasses and used his handkerchief to wipe the flecks of blood off them. Without the lenses his eyes were pale and defenseless and he let them pass over her lifeless body once before he replaced the frames and turned to Bobby Lee and Hiram. “Bury her with the others,” he said. “Boy, ain’t we havin’ some fun today?” Bobby Lee hooted, but the Misfit cut him off. “There’s no real pleasure in life,” he said sharply and walked back to the car.

Her voice, cracked and earnest, declared him as one of her own children, the statement hanging between them like a fragile thread in the stifling air. The Misfit’s pale eyes blinked behind thick glasses that reflected the distant sun, making him appear less man, more hollow instrument, tuned to discord. Hiram and Bobby Lee stood like rough-hewn statues, their hands idle but primed, their smirks a mockery of the tension thickening the moment. The grandmother’s outstretched hand shook with an urgency that seemed to belie her fragile clarity—a clarity forged by fear and sudden grace.Then came the shots, three in succession, each one punching the air with finality. Her body folded into the red clay ditch as if she were part of the earth all along, her hand still outstretched but now unyielding. A faint, enigmatic smile lingered on her lips, a puzzling counterpoint to the violence that had stilled her breath. The Misfit lowered his weapon slowly, his face twisted not in rage but something deeper—a silent rage turned inward, an unanswered question echoing in his marrow. He removed his glasses, wiped them carefully, and stared at the starkness of her lifeless form, his pale eyes vulnerable, almost raw.Bobby Lee chuckled, kicking a stone idly. “That was a fun one,” he said, his grin cruel. written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: The Misfit stood there with his black hat tilted back on his head and his eyes gleaming like two wet stones in the gathering dusk. His face was all angles and shadows, the kind that spoke of something gone wrong in the blood generations back. The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. "Take her with the others," he said, his voice flat as a snake's belly on hot pavement. Bobby Lee's face split in a yellow grin. "Some fun!" he said, but The Misfit's eyes had gone distant, like he was watching something terrible coming down the road toward them all. "It's no real pleasure in life," he said, and for a moment his face looked like it might crack open and show whatever darkness had been growing inside him since before he could remember. The sky above them was the exact color of a bruise, and somewhere in the distance a whip-poor-will called like it was mourning something that hadn't died yet.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: Standing on the yellow road in the bright sun, the grandmother before him and Hiram and Bobby Lee just behind, The Misfit sunk deeper into his bitter thinking. There can be no proof of anything—nothing earthly and nothing above—and certainly nothing like salvation for good deeds, or a father waiting and observing from some heavenly perch—and if there was no way to verify the existence of a real God, why live as if that God was watching? The Misfit wondered. The grandmother had on a hat with a brim that cast her face into aged shadows. Her mouth, a flat line, disturbed The Misfit and put a lump in his throat. But the grandmother’s face changed then, softened and clarified, and a beautiful smile spread from her to him. “You are one of my own children,” she said with great compassion, her voice loud and certain, outstretching feeble arms. The Misfit felt a wave of revulsion rising hot and tumorous in his chest and, recoiling, raised his gun and shot her three times. After, the grandmother’s body limp and lifeless in the ditch, the smile remained on her face. Even slumped, her hat upturned beside her, she had an air of perfect grace. Some question of forgiveness came then to The Misfit, which he carefully discarded and, taking off his glasses, surveyed her briefly with pale, defenseless eyes. “Get rid of her,” he told Hiram and Bobby Lee. “Put her with the others.” Bobby Lee chuckled, slapping Hiram on the shoulder, and said “Fun, real fun.” The Misfit turned cool eyes toward him, setting his jaw. “No, Bobby Lee,” he said, “it is not fun—not fun. There is no real pleasure in life.” He turned away from the body and walked on down the yellow road.

Where the original swings between the mundane, "she reached out and touched him on the shoulder," to the comparatively lyrical, "The Misfit sprang back as if a snake had bitten him and shot her three times through the chest." Later, in a particularly purple phrase, he's even "a specter in the twilight." At least in excerpt 2, we get closer to the mean grit of the original: "The Misfit turned his head and looked the grandmother in her eyes," and then later, captures the surprise of violence in "The Misfit took his gun out and shot her between her eyes, so that her nose was dashed away," where the descriptive "dashed away" does a lot of work to make us feel the Misfit's anger.
