written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Original: Valentine farm is a delusion. Who told you the negro deserved a place of refuge? Who told you that you had that right? Every minute of your life’s suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can’t exist. This place must be a delusion, too. Yet here we are.And America, too, is a delusion, the grandest one of all. The white race believes—believes with all its heart—that it is their right to take the land. To kill Indians. Make war. Enslave their brothers. This nation shouldn’t exist, if there is any justice in the world, for its foundations are murder, theft, and cruelty. Yet here we are.“I’m supposed to answer Mingo’s call for gradual progress, for closing our doors to those in need. I’m supposed to answer those who think this place is too close to the grievous influence of slavery, and that we should move west. I don’t have an answer for you. I don’t know what we should do. The word we. In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. It’s quite large. Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages. And that great mixture was brought to America in the holds of slave ships. To the north, the south. Their sons and daughters picked tobacco, cultivated cotton, worked on the largest estates and smallest farms. We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government. The word we. We are not one people but many different people. How can one person speak for this great, beautiful race—which is not one race but many, with a million desires and hopes and wishes for ourselves and our children?
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Reason: Excerpt One is closer to the original than Excerpt Two, largely because of its philosophical tone, sophisticated and weighty language, and its formality. The original is very formal, with slightly older language than contemporary/modern language: "Who told you that the negro deserved a place of refuge?... Every minute of your life's suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can't exist." Excerpt One adopts this rhetorical, sophisticated line of questioning, too: Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where we wouldn't follow?"  Excerpt 2 is much more muted and contemporary than this: "there was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people." That being said, I do feel like a bit of the language in Excerpt 1 is a bit too overblown and sophisticated, but it is definitely a closer match to the original than Excerpt 2.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.

Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. written_by_Cara.Original: It’s the mornings after the spider-and-heights dreams that are the most painful, that it takes sometimes three coffees and two showers and sometimes a run to loosen the grip on his soul’s throat; and these post-dream mornings are even worse if he wakes unalone, if the previous night’s Subject is still there, wanting to twitter, or to cuddle and, like, spoon, asking what exactly is the story with the foggy inverted tumblers on the bathroom floor, commenting on his night-sweats, clattering around in the kitchen, making kippers or bacon or something more hideous and unhoneyed he’s supposed to eat with post-coital male gusto, the ones who have this thing about they call it Feeding My Man, wanting a man who can barely keep down A.M. honey-toast to east with male gusto, elbows out and sovelling, making little noises. Even when alone, unable to uncurl alone and sit slowly up and wing out the sheet and go to the bathroom, these darkest mornings start days that Orin can’t even bring himself for hours to think about how he’ll get through the day. These worst mornings with cold floors and hot windows and merciless light — the soul’s certainty that the day will have to be not traversed but sort of climbed, vertically, and then that going to sleep again at the end of it will be like falling, again, off something tall and sheer.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: Orin’s mornings often began as a kind of existential residue, the aftermath of dreams that seemed to gnaw their way out from the deep recesses of the psyche’s cellar, dreams that were equal parts spiders and sheer verticality, both suffocating and vertiginous. The mornings required ritual, regimented almost to the point of ceremony: coffee brewed to a darkness that could rival the void, showers so scalding they left his skin reddened, runs that turned his lungs into bellows just to remind himself he was alive. Yet the presence of a Subject—the capital "S" both deliberate and derisive, a holdover from what Orin thought of as his internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance—would complicate the sequence. Subjects had a tendency toward earnest, unbidden gestures: talking as though morning were a shared phenomenon, attempting to wrap him in the tangled warmth of their limbs, even cooking eggs with a kind of oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive. The worst was the silence, the gap in conversation where their gaze hung too long on him, expectant. Alone, though, wasn’t better. The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2: Meanwhile, Orin’s nocturnally tormented with disturbing nightmares, dreams of falling through endless black space from great heights, or being chased by human-sized spiders, or sometimes both, dreams of enormous spiders pursuing him to a rooftop’s edge, from which he awakes totally emotionally drained and suffocated and physically drenched in sweat. Orin’s constructed a number of morning rituals to mitigate the queasy, sucked-out feeling his dreams give him, which rituals have grown more repetitive and elongated with time, such that he now needs to drink multiple cups of coffee, have two or sometimes three showers, and go on a run before he feels even remotely normal. On those mornings when he has a Subject still in his bed from the night before, and therefore for obvious reasons can’t indulge his full routine, he finds himself privately ruminating on his disturbing and repetitive nightmares while he and the Subject are cuddling, chatting or cooking breakfast together, all while she remains totally oblivious to his tormented internal state. So that paradoxically, waking up next to a partner actually makes him feel even greater discomfort and alienation than if he were alone. Though make no mistake, mornings alone are almost unbearably oppressive, even the routines do little to alleviate Orin’s dread of the day ahead, the coming day seeming to him alternately like an insurmountable vertical climb or yet another fall from a great height.
written_by_Cara.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original's voice and style than Excerpt 2 is. The language is darkly funny, complete with long, winding clauses that overlap and lock together, which perfectly mirrors the original. Excerpt 2 is a bit more direct and less winding, with several successive clauses that follow one another but not the same overlapping, stitched together feeling of the original excerpt. The vocabulary in the original, like the use of "kippers" or "unhoneyed" and "post coital male gusto" suggests a certain register that is echoed by Pargraph 1, with "oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive" and "internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance. Because of both sentence structure as well as language register, excerpt 1 is the better fit.

written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: Orin woke up next to the subject, mentally flaying himself for referring to this person as such, but using the same voice to berate himself that he used to describe this person as a subject, so the whole process became moot. The sheets were wrinkled and covered in little hairs, and Orin flinched as he recalled a dream of something cliche and horrid, spiders, heights, things rational only to the extent that they pose fear of what you can’t control (the venom, gravity,) and perhaps what you can (being a place with heights or spiders at all). The subject roused and pantomimed closeness, holding Orin’s clammy ribs, giggling at nothing, suggesting they fry or filet or bake the byproducts of various animals for breakfast. Orin’s beady little button eyes shimmered the reflections of the Subject's own eyes, through which they saw, perhaps, a glimpse of their own happiness, their own attempts at it, their own failures towards it. Orin longed to be alone, to return to his routines. Four coffees, each more burned than the last, a shower where he contemplated cleaning the mold spots that grew imperceptibly over the evening, perceptibly over the month, and perhaps a run after to justify the next day’s shower. But he knew that all of it, the loneliness, the mundane, was just a steep climb towards something crested and flat, a plain he wished to never see.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. The whole morning routine thing becoming this desperate assemblage of shields — the multiple coffees and showers and runs — against whatever nameless thing the dreams have excavated in him, and the presence of these "Subjects" (which is exactly the kind of clinically distant terminology someone would use when they're terrified of actual connection) only amplifies the awareness of his own emotional vacancy, which then of course makes him feel even more alienated, which then makes him need more coffee, etc., ad infinitum. That there's something almost liturgical about how he processes these mornings, these rituals of purification that never quite purify. The dreams themselves being less about actual spiders or heights than about the sensation of being watched while being alone, which is possibly the most contemporary form of existential terror there is. And it's worth noting that even in his solitude he's performing for some imagined audience, his anxiety itself becoming a kind of entertainment, the way everything does in our self-conscious age, even our own private sufferings being transformed into these sort of avant-garde performances for audiences that don't exist.
written_by_Stefan.Reason: I think E2 is closer to the original. The author employs some of the unusual sentence structures and grammatical tics that are characteristic of the original author, such as beginning sentences with “That”, using attenuating terms like “sort of” and “something like”, and using self-conscious narrative asides like “which is possibly the most contemporary form of existential terror there is” or “which is exactly the kind of clinically distant terminology someone would use”. E1 doesn’t really make use of these grammatical flourishes, and the inconsistent capitalization of “Subject” is very unlike the original author’s style. The original excerpt also talks generally about something that would and/or does often happen, as does P2, whereas E1 narrates a particular morning, which is inconsistent with the original style.

The subject roused and pantomimed closeness, holding Orin’s clammy ribs, giggling at nothing, suggesting they fry or filet or bake the byproducts of various animals for breakfast. Orin’s beady little button eyes shimmered the reflections of the Subject's own eyes, through which they saw, perhaps, a glimpse of their own happiness, their own attempts at it, their own failures towards it. Orin longed to be alone, to return to his routines. Four coffees, each more burned than the last, a shower where he contemplated cleaning the mold spots that grew imperceptibly over the evening, perceptibly over the month, and perhaps a run after to justify the next day’s shower. But he knew that all of it, the loneliness, the mundane, was just a steep climb towards something crested and flat, a plain he wished to never see.

written_by_Stefan.Original: It’s the mornings after the spider-and-heights dreams that are the most painful, that it takes sometimes three coffees and two showers and sometimes a run to loosen the grip on his soul’s throat; and these post-dream mornings are even worse if he wakes unalone, if the previous night’s Subject is still there, wanting to twitter, or to cuddle and, like, spoon, asking what exactly is the story with the foggy inverted tumblers on the bathroom floor, commenting on his night-sweats, clattering around in the kitchen, making kippers or bacon or something more hideous and unhoneyed he’s supposed to eat with post-coital male gusto, the ones who have this thing about they call it Feeding My Man, wanting a man who can barely keep down A.M. honey-toast to east with male gusto, elbows out and sovelling, making little noises. Even when alone, unable to uncurl alone and sit slowly up and wing out the sheet and go to the bathroom, these darkest mornings start days that Orin can’t even bring himself for hours to think about how he’ll get through the day. These worst mornings with cold floors and hot windows and merciless light — the soul’s certainty that the day will have to be not traversed but sort of climbed, vertically, and then that going to sleep again at the end of it will be like falling, again, off something tall and sheer.

written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. The whole morning routine thing becoming this desperate assemblage of shields — the multiple coffees and showers and runs — against whatever nameless thing the dreams have excavated in him, and the presence of these "Subjects" (which is exactly the kind of clinically distant terminology someone would use when they're terrified of actual connection) only amplifies the awareness of his own emotional vacancy, which then of course makes him feel even more alienated, which then makes him need more coffee, etc., ad infinitum. That there's something almost liturgical about how he processes these mornings, these rituals of purification that never quite purify. The dreams themselves being less about actual spiders or heights than about the sensation of being watched while being alone, which is possibly the most contemporary form of existential terror there is. And it's worth noting that even in his solitude he's performing for some imagined audience, his anxiety itself becoming a kind of entertainment, the way everything does in our self-conscious age, even our own private sufferings being transformed into these sort of avant-garde performances for audiences that don't exist.

written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Orin awoke in the cold post-dream anxiety and discomfort of a spider’s web, a fall from a height, a suffocating loss of control.  The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering.  Even multiple coffees, showers, or a morning run could barely rinse him of the feeling of being spectacularly tiny and yet at the mercy of something vast and unknowable.  Waking up alone was bad enough, but waking up with a Subject—an overnight guest whose name and details were best left unscrutinized—was a special kind of hell.The Subject, oblivious to the roiling psychic storm within him, would engage in the usual banalities of morning—the vapid small talk, the cuddling, the attempts at cooking breakfast.  Orin would lie there, trapped beneath the weight of their normalcy, feeling like a creature from another dimension.  Their cheerful voices sounded like the chirping of alien insects; their well-meaning touches were suffocating him.  Even when alone, these mornings were a bleak and desolate landscape.   The day stretched before him like a vertical climb or a fall, depending on the dream’s residue.  Either way, it was an ordeal to be endured, a performance to be staged.  The world was a stage, and he was a fraud—a fraud who longed for authenticity but found himself perpetually trapped in the performance of it.  The irony was not lost on him, but neither was it a source of amusement. It was simply a fact, as bleak and inescapable as the morning itself.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Orin wakes up feeling miserable. It’s always the same thing for him, that feeling of being wrenched out of a bottomless pit, the spiders, the heights, the tsunamis, the teeth falling out and clattering to the floor, the cliché and the boilerplate, dreams and fears so ordinary and yet completely destabilizing. He wants to go through his ritual, the multiple black coffees and the boiling hot shower and the run around the block in his sweatpants, just to get to a state resembling normalcy. But on this particular day, he has woken up next to a Subject, and he feels that rage, at the person he was last night, and also at the person lying in bed beside him. He has been doing this more and more lately, finding somebody to go to bed with, and he always hates himself for it. He wants to go back to the heights and the spiders to avoid the cuddling, the mindless small talk, the fried eggs, the depressing attempts at morning sex, the way the Subjects are chronically unable to recognize his torment. When he is alone, he feels suffocated, but with the Subjects, it’s worse. He wants to go back to the tall building he was teetering on the edge of the moment before he woke up, though now he feels, strangely, like he is already there. The subject rolls over and Orin imagines himself losing balance on that building, and tumbling through the agonizing, nauseating remainder of a lonely and empty day.
written_by_Celeste.Reason: Excerpt 2 is closer to the original than Excerpt 1. The original, for instance, is written in a combination of simple present ("the soul’s certainty that the day will have to be not traversed but sort of climbed") and habitual present ("these post-dream mornings are even worse if he wakes unalone"), lending Orin's feelings an aura of routine, suggesting to the reader that these grating events occur regularly. Excerpt 2 retains this impression, also using the simple present ("Orin wakes up feeling miserable") and the habitual present ("It’s always the same thing for him"). Excerpt 1, instead, relies on the past tense, losing that sense of urgency and rote repetition both. On the sentence level, Excerpt 2 approximates the labyrinthine, complex syntax of the original, with its several-clause-long sentences, its use of lists and concrete imagery, and its sparing use of figurative language. Excerpt 1, instead, uses more abstract imagery ("The tendrils of the dream clung to him, their grotesque forms and unspeakable anxieties lingering"), and relies too heavily on similes ("Orin would lie there, trapped beneath the weight of their normalcy, feeling like a creature from another dimension").

written_by_Renne_Flory.Original: The road went on through a shadeless burn and for miles there were only the charred shapes of trees in a dead land where nothing moved save windy rifts of ash that rose dolorous and died again down the blackened corridors.Late in the day the road brought him into a swamp. And that was all. Before him stretched a spectral waste out of which reared only the naked trees in attitudes of agony and dimly hominoid like figures in a landscape of the damned. A faintly smoking garden of the dead that tended away to the earth’s curve. He tried his foot in the mire before him and it rose in a vulvate welt claggy and sucking. He stepped back. A stale wind blew from this desolation and the marsh reeds and black ferns among which he stood clashed softly like things chained. He wondered why a road should come to such a place.Going back the way by which he came he met again the blind man tapping through the dusk. He waited very still by the side of the road, but the blind man passing turned his head and smiled upon him his blind smile. Holme watched him out of sight. He wondered where the blind man was going and did he know how the road ended. Someone should tell a blind man before setting him out that way.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Further along he passed into a swamp made up of naked trees and other dimly hominoid forms that moved too slowly and caught their breath at each others' fingerlike edges. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: The road lay before him, a trail of ash and dust, a ribbon unfurling through the skeletal remains of a forest.  Charred trees clawed at the sky, their branches like the limbs of the damned, twisted and broken.  The air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy on his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing.He ventured on, the road leading him into a swamp, a place where reality seemed to fray at the edges.  The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.

The lines that capture this for me are: "He tried his foot int he mire before him and it rose in a vulvate welt claggy and sucking. He stepped back." E2 captures this duality  "the air, thick with the taste of ash, lay heavy o his tongue, a grim reminder of the world's passing. He ventured on." E1 doesn't capture this balance between poeticality and simplicity as well.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Holme walked the ashen road beneath a sky gray and vast, its smothering pall hung with the promise of neither storm nor sun. The earth here was blasted, its countenance laid bare as if stripped of all pretense. Charred remains of trees thrust upward like the arms of the damned, skeletal, pleading to a god long deaf to their cries. The swamp loomed ahead, a blackened expanse of naked limbs clawing at the fading light, their dimly human shapes distorted by the oily gleam of the mire. He stepped forward, the ground yielding beneath his weight, a treacherous sucking sound rising with each motion. The air was heavy, each breath clotted with decay and rot, as if the place itself resisted intrusion. In the distance, the dry clash of wind-worried vegetation rose like the rattling of some unseen thing’s death throes. Holme turned back, his path winding like the arc of an indecipherable cipher. It was then he saw the blind man. A figure stooped yet unbroken, tapping his stick against the road’s edge, the sound of it like the faint metronome of a failing clock. Holme paused, watching. The blind man’s face was tilted skyward, the hollow sockets veiled in shadow, and yet a smile touched his lips as if he knew some secret. The man raised his face and Holme saw two voids where his eyes should be. Yet though he could not see Holme the blind man sensed him and smiled in greeting. written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: Holme kept to the road that wound long into a landscape of ash and cinder, charred trees skeletal in their moorings of roots twisting up through a hellscape of the dead. He walked on. Further on he came to a swamp that fell nightmarish on his eyes in all its nakedness of trees and dark figures dimly hominoid seemingly skulking in the mire. With a wary toe he tested the swampwater and reeled backwards at its unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation. He would not go this way. Retracing his steps back to the road and setting out upon it again he soon saw a man up ahead. The man tapped and swept a walking stick before him, feeling his way through that forever darkness only the blind knew the language of. The man smiled at Holme as he passed. Where the blind man was going Holme had already been, and Holme wondered then if anyone had informed the man of the grimness of what lay ahead at the end of the road. Walking on he lingered on what was not lost on him, the blind man’s incapability of seeing the burnt-out trees or even the road before him, not ever knowing where he’s going, but still following the road. No, he thought. He didn’t know where he was going.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: The road stretched out before Holme like a wound in the earth, ash drifting across its surface in spectral waves that moved without wind. The charred and twisted trees rose up from the swampland like ancient mariners frozen in their death throes, their blackened limbs reaching toward a colorless sky that held neither sun nor promise. He tested the mire with one boot and watched the earth shudder and contract like something alive yet unborn, the surface dimpling and rising again in slow persistent waves that spoke of depths best left unplumbed. Through the dead forest came a sound like bones rattling, though there was nothing there but naked branches clicking together in a wind that seemed to carry voices. Then came the blind man, tapping his way along the road's edge with a stick worn smooth as glass, his face lifted in permanent expectation, smiling as if he knew some secret that the seeing world had lost. Holme watched him pass, this prophet of the wastes, and thought how the man's blindness might be a mercy in such a place as this. For what use were eyes in a world become nothing but ash and shadow, where even the trees had forgotten their own names and stood like sentinels at the gates of some darker realm that lay just beyond the next bend in the road, waiting with infinite patience for travelers who would never return.

While both paragraphs emulate the original's emphasis on establishing the tone through warped natural imagery, Excerpt 1 also mirrors the original author's balance of imagery, characterization, and internal monologue. This can be seen in how both the original author and Excerpt 1 establish the image without further authorial flourish, moving onto the character's actions and reflections. For instance, "unsure footing of bog and moss, crags of rock wet against the backdrop of windcurrents clashing the sodden vegetation and his feeling of desolation" matches both the visual descriptiveness but spareness of speculation/philosophizing in "a dead land where nothing moved save windy rifts o ash that rose dolorous and died again down the blackened corridors.

Beyond its reliance on overused tropes of "blind men who see deeper", it also doesn't match the original's simple description of the man as blind without further pontification or explanation.

written_by_Benjamin.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.

E1 uses figurative language that the original does not, such as: "painted in shades of amber and violet" and "dust particles dance in the afternoon light." E2 is much more straightforward: "But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to."

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling my close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.
written_by_James_Cato.Reason: The original reads more like an anecdote and tribute to the narrator's father. Excerpt 1 achieves this better than Excerpt 2. Excerpt 1 is direct, and its diction and sentence structure is closer to the original. Excerpt 2 employs several similes and metaphors, conditional phrasing and details feelings ("a voice steadied by conviction" and "precision of his faith") whereas the original names feelings rather simply using plain adjectives instead of describing them ("into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion," "received with such great happiness," "father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence"). Excerpt 1 and both original end with the father's death and returns the focus to the father.

written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt1: The weight of the manuscript, a physical embodiment of years of creative struggle, felt familiar and foreign in my hands. written_by_Devanshi.Original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.
written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt1: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.
written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: It was a winter morning thick with silence, the kind that stretches across frozen earth, hollow and unforgiving. My mother knelt on the cold wooden floor, her breath visible in the brittle air as she arranged the meager preparations she could muster. A pot of water on the stove, its steam curling upward like the last prayers of the desperate, her trembling hands struggling with scissors dulled by time. In the dim light, the pale fabric she had cut into a crude gown seemed to shiver, as though alive with the sorrow that filled the room. Pain ripped through her body like a jagged knife, forcing her onto her knees, but her face, pale and drawn, bore the stoic determination of someone who knew that the world would not offer her mercy. The moment of birth arrived, primal and raw, a soundless rupture of the fragile divide between life and death. She held the newborn close, her whispered pleas breaking against the unyielding silence. "Live," she murmured, a chant that carried the weight of her being. For one fragile heartbeat, the child stirred, its existence fleeting, a candle flickering in a relentless wind. Then it was gone, leaving behind only its weightless absence. My mother sat there, cradling the lifeless form, her own warmth seeping into the icy floor. The stillness settled over her like a shroud, and in that moment, the world outside ceased to exist.
written_by_Devanshi.Reason: P1 is closer because it captures the simple poeticality of the original more so than P2, which goes overboard with figurative language.  In the original, every detail is spare and precise: "bloodied little body" and "the cold gradually leach into the flesh." There is no overblown symbolism or philosophical musing. E2 has phrases like "pain tripped through her body like a jagged knife," "the stoic determination," and "the fragile divide between life and death." It is too poetic, too overcooked. E1 retains the simplicity: "blood-covered" and "seeped into her body."

She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: That winter night, my mother told me, was like a blade of ice pressed against her spine. The scissors lay sterilized in boiling water, steam rising like ghostly breath in the dim room, while her trembling hands folded and refolded the small white gown she'd fashioned from scraps in her sewing box. When the pain came, it was not like anything living – it was ancient, prehistoric, like continents being torn apart. She bit down on a rolled cloth, her screams collapsing inward, becoming part of her flesh, part of the darkness. The umbilical cord, when she finally cut it, was purple-blue like twilight, like the last moment before complete darkness. She held the tiny body, so light it could have been made of paper, chanting words that weren't words but rather the sound of her soul trying to transfer its own life force. For one heartbeat, maybe two, the baby's chest rose – a movement so slight it could have been the shadow of hope itself. Then stillness. The floor's cold crept up through her body like rising water, until she too became still, became ice, became the very essence of winter itself. Her warmth retreated inward, as though trying to follow her child into that place beyond reaching.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_Devin.Reason: Option 1 uses poetic language in a way the original doesn’t. It overreaches and ends up feeling a bit performative – “the baby's chest rose – a movement so slight it could have been the shadow of hope itself,” or “the very essence of winter itself.” The original is effective because it’s so restrained and clear: “She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made… For god’s sake don’t die.” Option 2 is flat in a way the original isn’t either. It paraphrases the scene without capturing its emotional weight or specificity. It says: “her newborn child went still and died,” which is technically accurate but misses the pacing and quiet terror of: “Around an hour later, the baby was dead.” Neither version really gets there, but if I had to choose, I’d say Option 2. It’s less distracting, even if it’s too muted.

There is a similarly short, staccato quality to the sentences, and similarly unadorned language, in the Original and in Excerpt2. For example, 

Original: "She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. Whereas Excerpt1 features more vivid language, and more figurative language, simile and metaphor, etc. In the Original, the mother's contractions are simply contractions; in Excerpt2, they are "waves of pain." The baby's fleeting heartbeat is "the shadow of hope itself." The cold is "the very essence of winter itself." This gives it all a (melo)dramatic quality that the Original does not have.

written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously.  The air, thick with the metallic scent of life and death, echoed her ragged breaths, each one a desperate prayer.  She had become a primal vessel, fear and pain etching lines on her face, a grotesque map of motherhood.  The room, a battlefield of sweat and tears, cradled the echo of her final push, the newborn’s slippery form a dark miracle against the faded floorboards.  With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.Her voice, hoarse and raw, filled the silence, a chant for life, a plea to whatever gods might be listening.  But the newborn’s cry, a fleeting spark in the vast emptiness, was swallowed by the shadows.  The silence returned, heavier now, crushing her with its finality.  She clutched the lifeless body to her breast, her warmth a futile offering to the cold stillness that had settled over them.  The world outside continued its relentless march, oblivious to the silent tragedy unfolding within those walls.  The floor, cold and unforgiving, seeped into her bones, mirroring the icy grip of grief that threatened to consume her.
written_by_Rachael.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original's voice and style. The original is straightforward (ex. "My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors."), only using figurative language at important moments (ex. "and held the whimpering scrap in her arms."). Excerpt 2 uses a great deal of strange and ineffective figurative language (ex. "The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously." and "With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.") that significantly differs from the original's voice. Excerpt 1, though not perfectly consistent, is much more consistent with the orignal's voice and style than Excerpt 2, using figurative language much more sparingly and with more purpose (ex. "A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.")

written_by_Cara.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I closed my eyes and thought about the nature of longing, how it shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel, becoming more precise in its form the more complete the void becomes. Sylvie had left in that way of hers, without sound or ceremony, as if she had simply dissolved into the thick afternoon air, and I found myself studying the treeline where the shadows gathered, imagining her watching me pretend not to notice the solitude she had left behind. There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: Excerpt1 is slightly more in-line with the tone of the original excerpt. Excerpt2 speaks more vaguely and metaphorically ("how it shapes itself around absence like water flowing into an empty vessel") where the original is more functional and plain-spoken even as it is beautiful. I also prefer the ending of paragraph1, allowing the image to linger as opposed to stating outright what it is attempting to describe, though it lacks the nuance and contraditction of the original.

There is something about craving that makes the thing craved more vivid than itself could ever be—like the memory of a wild berry's tartness being sweeter than the actual taste, or how the thought of rain can feel more quenching than the drops themselves when they finally fall. I began to imagine crafting a statue, not of cold marble but of living stone that would draw up minerals from the earth like a tree draws sap, and I would place her among the pines where the light filters down in dusty columns. Unlike Lot's wife, who turned to salt in her backward glance of regret, this woman would be adorned with rare blooms that only grow in the deepest parts of the forest, and her face would hold all the forgiveness that Lot's wife could never find. The wild children—for there are always wild children in these woods, moving like shadows between the trees—would gather around her feet, marveling at the strange flowers that crown her head, at the way her stone hands, though forever still, seem to reach for them with infinite tenderness. They would sense in her something of mothers they barely remember, of homes they might have had in some other life, and they would leave small offerings at her feet: interesting pebbles, abandoned birds' nests, fragments of colored glass that catch the light like trapped pieces of sky. And I thought perhaps this is what Sylvie and I were both seeking: not the thing itself, but the holy shape of its absence, which holds more truth than presence ever could.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: The original excerpt uses elaborate and lyrical language to reflect on the nature of craving; the passage moves from philosophical musing to hyper-specific daydreaming about building a woman out of snow in the forest, replete with mythic/Biblical references. Each use of figurative language is elaborated upon, turned into its own sensory experience: "Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries." The first excerpt matches this philosophical contemplation. much more closely: "I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want" (p1); "To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it" (original).
