written_by_Connor.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt1: It was the longing itself that seemed to summon the essence of what I desired, as if yearning were a prayer that the world, in its quiet way, conspired to answer. The sweetness of berries unpicked lingered in the air, more vibrant for being out of reach. Sylvie had vanished again, her silence as deliberate as a shadow retreating with the sun, and I knew not to call for her. It was better to let the absence settle, to imagine her slender frame paused just out of sight, watching from the line of trees, her face half-lit by the dappled sun. The woods held their breath, alive with the hum of insects and the rustle of unseen creatures, and I found myself wondering if she had gone into them to become something wilder, freer, more elemental than her mortal self. It was then I imagined a statue, a woman wrought from the alabaster of my mind, her form unyielding yet softened by an artist’s hand. Her hair, an eternal cascade of rare blossoms, reached toward the ground like a benediction. She would not be like Lot’s wife, turned back toward despair, but a figure of grace, fixed in forgiveness, her face turned forward into the eternal now.Around her feet would gather children, wild-eyed and untamed, the sort that flit through the forest like whispers of untold stories. They would marvel at her beauty, her quiet presence, her promise of solace, though her hands, stiff and unyielding, could never stroke their hair or lift them from their loneliness. And yet, the children would linger, imagining themselves known, loved, by the depths of her unseeing gaze. Perhaps Sylvie, wherever she was, could understand such a figure—one who existed between the realms of presence and absence, neither gone nor wholly there. The trees would hold her as their own, casting shadows that shifted like whispers against her alabaster skin. And I, rooted in my own solitude, could only wonder if longing itself was a form of creation, if absence was a kind of grace, and if Sylvie’s silence spoke a language deeper than words.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt2: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.

Excerpt 1 succeeds the best in capturing the more lyrical register of the original, where it seems like it's mimicking the bible, which seems like the most essential facet of the original voice. "It was the longing itself that seemed to summon the essence of what I desired, as if yearning were a prayer that the world, in its quiet way, conspired to answer."

Excerpt 2, by contrast, captures the curtness of the original, but not the biblical lyricism: "Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. written_by_Sophia.Original: History has failed us, but no matter.At the turn of the century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. Both were born and raised in the fishing village of Yeongdo—a five-mile-wide islet beside the port city of Busan. In their long marriage, the wife gave birth to three sons, but only Hoonie, the eldest and the weakest one, survived. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot; he was, however, endowed with hefty shoulders, a squat build, and a golden complexion. Even as a young man, he retained the mild, thoughtful temperament he’d had as a child. When Hoonie covered his misshapen mouth with his hands, something he did out of habit meeting strangers, he resembled his nice-looking father, both having the same large, smiling eyes. Inky eyebrows graced his broad forehead, perpetually tanned from outdoor work. Like his parents, Hoonie was not a nimble talker, and some made the mistake of thinking that because he could not speak quickly there was something wrong with his mind, but that was not true.In 1910, when Hoonie was twenty-seven years old, Japan annexed Korea.The fisherman and his wife, thrifty and hardy peasants, refused to be distracted by the country’s incompetent aristocrats and corrupt rulers, who had lost their nation to thieves. When the rent for their house was raised again, the couple moved out of their bedroom and slept in the anteroom near the kitchen to increase the number of lodgers.The wooden house they had rented for over three decades was not large, just shy of five hundred square feet. Sliding paper doors divided the interior into three snug rooms, and the fisherman himself had replaced its leaky grass roof with reddish clay tiles to the benefit of his landlord, who lived in splendor in a mansion in Busan. Eventually, the kitchen was pushed out to the vegetable garden to make way for the larger cooking pots and the growing number of portable dining tables that hung on pegs along the mortared stone wall.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo, the small fishing village near Busan where they had lived all their lives. Their eldest son Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, had survived while his two younger brothers had not. The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature. His parents had learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed – whether it was their son's conditions or the failures of their aristocratic rulers. When the rent increased again, they simply moved their own bedroom into the garden to make space for more lodgers, converting their former sleeping quarters into another room to let. Their kitchen now occupied a corner of the vegetable garden, the warm cooking smoke rising past clay roof tiles toward the evening sky. Some mornings, while preparing the lodgers' breakfast, the fisherman's wife would pause to watch the boats heading out to sea, their white sails bright against the gray dawn. She never envied the landlord's mansion in Busan with its Western furnishings and grand gates. Their modest wooden house with its sliding paper doors held everything they needed – space enough for lodgers whose rent helped them survive, a garden that provided vegetables for their soup, and most importantly, their son Hoonie, whose quiet strength and kind heart made their lives worth living. The other villagers often remarked on the family's fortitude, though the fisherman and his wife saw nothing remarkable in their way of life. To them, each day was simply another opportunity to work, to care for their son, and to maintain their dignity in a world that increasingly seemed to value only wealth and status. In Korea, as in most places, survival meant adapting to change without losing oneself, and this family had mastered that delicate balance through years of practiced resilience.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: Excerpt 1 often strays from the language and tone found in the original excerpt; we see this most keenly in the formal language of the sentence, "The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature." The original describes Hoonie as such: "Even as a young man, he retained the mild, thoughtful temperament he’d had as a child"; a long shot from excerpt 1, with the exception of the semi-formal "retained". written_by_Tian.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.
written_by_Tian.Excerpt2: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.

written_by_Lara_Wass.Original: Much later, after she had left her husband and lived several years with Jean-Marc, she was at the seashore one day: they were dining outdoors, on a wooden deck over the water; she retains an intense memory of whiteness: the deck, the tables, the chairs, the tablecloths, everything was white, the lampposts were painted white and the bulbs beamed a white light against the summer sky, not yet dark, where the moon, itself white too, was whitening everything around them. And in this bath of white she was struck by a feeling of unbearable nostalgia for Jean-Marc. Nostalgia? How could she feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her? How can you suffer from the absence of a person who is present? (Jean-Marc knew how to answer that: you can suffer nostalgia in the presence of the beloved if you glimpse a future where the beloved is no more; if the beloved’s death is, invisibly, already present.) During that moment of strange nostalgia at the seaside, she suddenly thought of her dead child, and a wave of happiness flooded over her. Soon she would be frightened by this feeling. But no one can do a thing about feelings, they exist and there’s no way to censor them. We can reproach ourselves for some action, for a remark, but not for a feeling, quite simply because we have no control at all over it.
written_by_Lara_Wass.Excerpt1: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? She had left him because she wanted to; to be with the man she loved. The man sitting across from her now, handsome in a white button-down shirt. It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.
written_by_Lara_Wass.Excerpt2: She sat across from Jean-Marc at the seaside restaurant, her fingers tracing invisible patterns on the white linen tablecloth, as if trying to anchor herself amidst the overwhelming brightness surrounding them. The deck stretched out, pale and gleaming, the lampposts shimmered like ghostly sentinels, and the moon hung low, casting an iridescent glow that seemed to swallow every color except white. The air was still, suffused with the faint, rhythmic whispers of the tide. Jean-Marc watched her, his expression serene yet attentive, as if he could read the kaleidoscope of emotions dancing behind her eyes. She felt a paradoxical pang of nostalgia—sharp and bittersweet—as though mourning something lost, though everything she cherished sat mere inches away. It puzzled her, this longing, this melancholy wrapped in an inexplicable happiness. Was it the memory of her deceased child, flitting unbidden into her mind like a shadow across the moonlight? Or was it the fear of losing Jean-Marc, his presence so vital it seemed like a delicate thread connecting her to the world? She smiled suddenly, a fleeting expression of joy so pure it frightened her. Jean-Marc reached for her hand, silently acknowledging the fragile beauty of her emotion. In that luminous moment, it struck her: we are masters of our actions, perhaps even of our words, but not of our feelings, those wild, untamed creatures that move within us, defying reason and will.

written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.

Just roll the roof back and screw it on, grease the face with white tanning butter and move out with the music at top volume, and at least a pint of ether.Getting hold of the drugs had been no problem, but the car and the tape recorder were not easy things to round up at 6:30 on a Friday afternoon in Hollywood. I already had one car, but it was far too small and slow for desert work. We want one of those new Belgian Heliowatts with a voice—activated shotgun mike, for picking up conversations in oncoming cars." We made several more calls and finally located our equip—ment in a store about five miles away. It was closed, but the salesman said he would wait, if we hurried. But we were de—layed en route when a Stingray in front of us killed a pedestrian on Sunset Boulevard. The store was closed by the time we got there. There were people inside, but they refused to come to the double—glass door until we gave it a few belts and made ourselves clear.“Finally two salesmen brandishing tire irons came to the door and we managed to negotiate the sale through a tiny slit. Then they opened the door just wide enough to shove the equipment out, before slamming and locking it again. "Now take that stuff and get the hell away from here," one of them shouted through the slit
written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: The attorney was on the phone, his voice a guttural rasp against the faux-Polynesian backdrop of the bar. "Red," he barked, "not pink. And make it snappy, the goddamn plane leaves in three hours."  I swiveled on the barstool, the vinyl squeaking in protest, and surveyed the wreckage of our preparations. Empty Mai Tai glasses stood like fallen soldiers, casualties in the war against sobriety. A crumpled napkin bore the cryptic message,"Convertible. Red. Not a goddamn boat."Outside, the Hollywood sun beat down with the malevolence of a loan shark. A pack of tourists shuffled past, their eyes glazed over with the vacant stare of the terminally sunburned. A low-slung Stingray roared by, leaving behind the faint scent of burnt rubber and the echo of a scream.  "Jesus," I muttered, "this town is a goddamn meat grinder."The attorney slammed the phone down, his face a mask of grim determination. "Got it," he snarled, "a red convertible. Picking it up in an hour."  He fixed me with a bloodshot stare. "Now, about that recording equipment..."We found the electronics store tucked away in a seedy strip mall, sandwiched between a bail bondsman and an adult bookstore. The salesmen eyed us with the suspicion of a pit bull eyeing a poodle. "We're closed," one growled, brandishing a tire iron."Bullshit," the attorney snarled back, "we just need some high-quality recording equipment. And we're in a hurry."  The door cracked open a few inches, revealing a glimpse of darkened aisles and the glint of chrome. A hand emerged, clutching a hefty price list. "Cash only," a voice rasped.An hour later, we emerged from the store, blinking against the harsh sunlight. The attorney clutched a bag crammed with microphones, recorders, and enough batteries to power a small city. I hefted a suitcase filled with enough "heinous chemicals" to fuel a weekend-long bender.We piled into the waiting convertible, the red paint gleaming like a fresh coat of blood. The attorney gunned the engine, and we roared off into the desert, leaving behind the madness of Hollywood and heading towards the even greater madness of Las Vegas.  The wind whipped through our hair, carrying with it the scent of freedom and the promise of adventure. This was the Gonzo life, and we were riding it full throttle, straight into the heart of the American Dream.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: My life felt chaotic, and I decided the best way to deal with this would be to go on a reckless drive while indulging in loads and loads of heinous chemicals. We decided we would drive from Hollywood to Vegas, and I began to round up all my drugs—mescaline, amyl, and half a jar of cocaine that I had been keeping in my coat closet for a special occasion. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.

Just roll the roof back and screw it on, grease the face with white tanning butter and move out with the music at top volume, and at least a pint of ether.Getting hold of the drugs had been no problem, but the car and the tape recorder were not easy things to round up at 6:30 on a Friday afternoon in Hollywood. I already had one car, but it was far too small and slow for desert work. We went to a Polynesian bar, where my attorney made seventeen calls before locating a convertible with adequate horsepower and proper coloring. "Hang onto it," I heard him say into the phone. "We’ll be over to make the trade in thirty minutes." Then after a pause, he began shouting: "What? Of course the gentleman has a major credit card! Do you realize who the fuck you’re talking to?" "Don’t take any guff from these swine," I said as he slammed the phone down. "Now we need a sound store with the finest equipment. Nothing dinky. We want one of those new Belgian Heliowatts with a voice—activated shotgun mike, for picking up conversations in oncoming cars." We made several more calls and finally located our equip—ment in a store about five miles away. It was closed, but the salesman said he would wait, if we hurried. But we were de—layed en route when a Stingray in front of us killed a pedestrian on Sunset Boulevard. The store was closed by the time we got there. There were people inside, but they refused to come to the double—glass door until we gave it a few belts and made ourselves clear.“Finally two salesmen brandishing tire irons came to the door and we managed to negotiate the sale through a tiny slit. Then they opened the door just wide enough to shove the equipment out, before slamming and locking it again. "Now take that stuff and get the hell away from here," one of them shouted through the slit
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender. I was hallucinating a chase and knew any dip in speed would end my life. My life was behind me, chemicals were in front of me and inside me, and this gave me some real pep as the tires screamed down the asphalt trail. The attorney sat in the passenger seat, even more delusional, leaning and bending with the rapidly changing momentum of the vehicle like an inflatable man. We went over a rock with a terrible chunking sound, and he didn't even wince as I turned us back toward the street and away from the cacti and boiled soil stretching endlessly around us. We were leaving Hollywood and aiming vaguely for Las Vegas. We rarely consulted maps or asked for directions. We would get there. The attorney slammed another acid tab into his mouth. The car, I realized, wouldn't do at all. It was too slow and too compact. It was terrible. What we needed was a big, rumbling convertible. We stopped for a few drinks at an ugly Polynesian bar, and the attorney made some frantic calls about a new rental, demanding the respect an esquire deserves. He did it. We turned off at a rental joint to turn in our desecrated piece of crap for a nice new Stingray. The salesman haggled with us, thinking we couldn't haggle back under the grip of heinous chemicals. We also required some high-quality recording equipment, which we would find when we finally tore into Vegas. There was something we needed it for, because this was a work trip, and all our expenses were dutifully covered as long as we did the interviews. We tried to enter an electronics store, and the clerk stopped us. "Go away," he said, holding the door shut. He waved a crowbar. The attorney negotiated quickly, sneaking company credit cards through the crack, and shortly after, recording equipment sat on the curb with us. We lay there, basking in the motion of our minds, when a Stingray convertible bashed into an elder across the road and left him to die.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: The plan was simple—if you could call it that—get the car, get the gear, and get out before anybody realized we were far too gone to be handling lethal machinery. My attorney had a phone jammed to his ear, barking demands at a salesman who clearly wanted nothing more than to shove a tire iron through his skull. “We need a convertible, the biggest one you’ve got. No, don’t give me that Chevy Impala bullshit, I want something with horsepower, something that howls like a dying wolf on the open road.” I could see the man on the other end hesitating, sensing that this was a deal he wanted no part of, but the law was clear—money talks, and we had just enough to sound legitimate. Meanwhile, across the room, a Stingray had just mowed down some poor bastard on Sunset Boulevard, the last frantic gasps of air leaking out of his ruined lungs as people stood around pretending not to see. My attorney watched, nodding approvingly, as if this was part of the deal. “That’s efficiency,” he muttered. I took a long drag from my cigarette and checked the time—not because it mattered, but because it felt important to note that this day had already spun out of control and it wasn’t even noon. The air smelled like hot asphalt and tequila. The salesmen were jittery now, fumbling with the equipment we needed—high-quality recording gear, something we could use to document the horrors we were bound to encounter in Vegas. The door cracked open just enough for us to reach through and grab our loot, an unspoken agreement that we would disappear into the desert and never return. “Load it up,” my attorney barked, shoving a crumpled wad of cash through the gap. “And throw in a few extra tapes. I have a feeling we’re going to need them.” He grinned like a man on the verge of a spectacular crime, then turned to me. “Time to move. The road waits for no one.” I nodded, already feeling the rush, the weight of reckless momentum pulling us forward. It was go-time, and there was no turning back.
written_by_James_Cato.Reason: Much like the original passage, Excerpt 1 is frenetic, breathless, and even vicious. From the original, "Every now and then when your life gets complicated and the weasels start closing in, the only real cure is to load up on heinous chemicals and then drive like a bastard from Hollywood to Las Vegas." From Excerpt 1, "I was driving at an absurd speed and trying my best to keep to the road—though I could be excused for the rumbling moments when I veered into the orange moonscape, because it didn't matter at all as long as you didn't mind a few dings in your fender." The flippant, careless, untethered style is seamlessly integrated into the content of Excerpt 1, which is admittedly structured differently from the original but contains the same key Thompson essence. In Excerpt 2, the flippancy feels slightly less natural, the movement between ideas punctuated by dialogue with the attorney that alters the free-flowing stream-of-consciousness. There are also two insertions bracketed by em dashes in Excerpt 2 that imply a hesitancy we don't see in Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas: "—if you could call it that—" and "—not because it mattered."

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Christ almighty, here we are - trapped in this feverish documentation of a madman's journey, watching the words crawl across the page like speed-crazed insects searching for meaning in the neon wasteland between Hollywood and Vegas. The story reeks of desperate chemicals and the acrid stench of burning rubber on asphalt, all wrapped up in the frenzied quest for the Great American Convertible. My attorney, that chrome-domed harbinger of chaos, is barking into payphones at terrified salesmen while I hover near the bar of some godforsaken Polynesian tomb, mainlining Singapore Slings and wondering if we'll ever make it out of LA alive. The whole scene has the surgical precision of a hurricane - first the maniac phone calls, then the ugly business with the recording equipment, and somewhere in between, the grotesque spectacle of that poor bastard getting mowed down by a Stingray on Sunset. Jesus, what a place. What a time. The salesmen are wielding tire irons now, passing our gear through a crack in the door like they're feeding raw meat to a cage full of rabid wolverines. Can't blame them, really - not with what's happening out there in the streets. The whole country's gone belly-up with fear and loathing, and here we are, two professional journalists, supposedly documenting this circus of depravity. But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong. The evidence is everywhere: in the twisted metal on Sunset, in the paranoid eyes of the salesmen, in the heinous chemicals coursing through our bloodstreams like electric eels in a bathtub. And somehow we're supposed to make sense of it all, turn it into something resembling journalism. What a goddamn joke. But there's no going back now - we've bought the ticket, and by God, we're going to take the ride.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: With everything so fucked, there wasn't much to do but the usual heinous chemicals. Preparation for some kind of proper drive, driving on to forever and just past it. We were trying to find a suitable convertible and some recording equipment, but none of it was going well. The attorney met me at the Polynesian bar, and I was calling up the company, asking if I could get my good equipment and how soon. They weren't making sense—you could rarely make sense with these people—but the attorney grabbed the phone, and it seemed like soon enough we'd get it squared away. But the car situation was harder; the salesman took one look at us and shut down, as if we weren't respectable people with respectable money. The attorney stepped in again and got it sorted in his sweaty, loud, unpleasant sort of way. Some people just commanded respect. At the equipment store, we were hovering halfway in and halfway out while the salesman, tire irons in his hands like we were common thieves, was trying to get all our information from us pronto, and the motherfucker wouldn't even open the door. I kept saying I was just there for my equipment, and finally, exasperated, he came back with the stuff we'd asked for, sliding it through like a file in a prison cake. Just as we got in the car, we saw a Stingray hit a pedestrian on Sunset Boulevard. Real quick, it happening in a single breath—though I guessed the pedestrian wouldn't be breathing again after this accident. I looked at the attorney, and he laughed, shell-shocked, and I laughed too even though he was driving me crazy. After an hour on the road, he was still driving me crazy in the passenger seat. We did a little peyote and then a little ketamine, and I thought the two cancelled each other out, for the most part, and my foot was flat on the wheel. All around us we saw desert brush and mesas and nothing, the flat orange nothing that lived out there in the desert. Hollywood felt far away then, but Las Vegas felt further, and we hadn't done much by way of preparations for this Las Vegas trip. But the highway stretched out blissfully before us... and the drugs were good, real good. Sunset would come in a quick green flash.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: Excerpt 2 is closer to the content of the original—whereas Excerpt 1 talks about a "story" and describes the narrator as being "trapped in this feverish documentation of a madman's journey, watching the words crawl across the page like speed-crazed insects searching for meaning in the neon wasteland between Hollywood and Vegas," there is no mention of words on a page or a madman's journey in the original excerpt. Excerpt 2 mentions drugs by name ("peyote," "ketamine,") just like the original which mentions "ether." Excerpt 1, however, only talks about "heinous chemicals." In addition, Excerpt 1 makes a diversion to talk about the "American Dream gone wrong," which feels too general compared to the original excerpt, which is mostly just narrating a series of events. Excerpt 2 stays closer to the original by mostly only describing the characters' attempts to rent a car and drive out into the desert.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Original: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off their hinges; Rumpelmayer’s men were coming. And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning — fresh as if issued to children on a beach.What a lark! What a plunge! For so it had always seemed to her, when, with a little squeak of the hinges, which she could hear now, she had burst open the French windows and plunged at Bourton into the open air. How fresh, how calm, stiller than this of course, the air was in the early morning; like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet (for a girl of eighteen as she then was) solemn, feeling as she did, standing there at the open window, that something awful was about to happen; looking at the flowers, at the trees with the smoke winding off them and the rooks rising, falling; standing and looking until Peter Walsh said, “Musing among the vegetables?”— was that it? —“I prefer men to cauliflowers”— was that it? He must have said it at breakfast one morning when she had gone out on to the terrace — Peter Walsh. He would be back from India one of these days, June or July, she forgot which, for his letters were awfully dull; it was his sayings one remembered; his eyes, his pocket-knife, his smile, his grumpiness and, when millions of things had utterly vanished — how strange it was! — a few sayings like this about cabbages.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Mrs. Dalloway, stepping out into the June morning, thought how she would fetch the flowers herself, for Lucy had quite enough to manage with those men from Rumpelmayer's coming. The fresh air caught her face (how young she felt, how perpetually astonished!) and sent her mind spinning back to Bourton, to those mornings when she was eighteen, when she would burst out onto the terrace and feel the world pause, crystalize, become both solemn and effervescent in that early hour. Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.

From the original, "How fresh, how calm, stiller than this of course, the air was in the early morning; like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet (for a girl of eighteen as she then was) solemn...". Excerpt 1 conveys this sentiment "The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery." written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt1: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Outside, it was almost Bourton—the air was sharp, like a country wind, she thought; at eighteen, in Bourton, it had felt more like a gale; yes, at eighteen years old, simply placing one foot in front of the other had lent Clarissa purpose—a stroll around the garden was as grand as an expedition to India. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.

written_by_Brianna.Excerpt1: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.
written_by_Brianna.Excerpt2: Clarissa Dalloway, a woman of exquisite sensibility, stepped out into the vibrant London morning. She had decided to buy the flowers herself, a small act of consideration for Lucy, her servant, who was already bustling about with the preparations for the evening's gathering. The crisp air carried a hint of the past, and Clarissa's thoughts drifted back to Bourton, her childhood home. She remembered the mornings there, the dew still clinging to the roses, the world awakening with a freshness that was both exhilarating and solemn.At eighteen, the world had seemed to stretch before her, a tapestry woven with infinite possibilities. Now, years later, the edges of that tapestry had frayed. But some threads remained bright, indelible marks on the fabric of her memory. Peter Walsh, with his sardonic wit and his penchant for the dramatic, was one such thread. "I prefer men to cauliflowers," he had declared one morning at breakfast, his eyes twinkling with amusement.Clarissa smiled at the memory. Peter was returning from India soon, his letters filled with tales of his adventures and misadventures. He was a man of contradictions, capable of great passion and profound melancholy. Clarissa had always found him both exasperating and endearing. His return would stir the waters of her well-ordered life, she knew, but it was a disruption she welcomed. For Peter, with all his flaws and foibles, reminded her of a time when life was less predictable, less constrained by the conventions of society. He was a relic of her youth, a symbol of a time when her heart was still open to the world, before the disappointments and disillusionments of adulthood had begun to close in.
written_by_Brianna.Reason: While neither passage quite emulates Woolf at the sentence-level, Excerpt 1 includes a lightness and questioning that mirrors the original more effectively. Woolf writes, "And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning — fresh as if issued to children on a beach. What a lark! What a plunge!" From Excerpt 1, "The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? written_by_Stefan.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. written_by_Stefan.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: The Black Panther Party, a whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury, had been my crucible. I'd joined partly to prove a point, to silence the whispers that trailed me like a shadow. "Not Black enough," they hissed, both Black and white voices mingling in a chorus of disapproval. My crime? Muttering "Egads" during a heated basketball game, perhaps. Or maybe it was my novels, those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus, drawing accusations of elitism and worse, cultural betrayal. One particularly scathing review declared, "His Aeschylus is a betrayal of his Black heritage, a misguided attempt to elevate himself above his roots." The New York literary party, a swirling vortex of ambition and pretense, was no different. A literary agent, her eyes scanning the room for the next big thing, dismissed my work with a wave of her hand. "Forget Aeschylus," she scoffed, "write true, gritty real stories of Black life. That's what sells." I wanted to retort, "My life, my experience, isn't that Black enough for you?" But the words caught in my throat, choked by the weight of expectation. The agent, sensing my hesitation, moved on, her attention snagged by a performance artist reciting a monologue about the Black experience. The irony was thick enough to cut with a knife.  Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.
written_by_James_Braun.Reason:
The original combines an erudite precision with a cutting wit to produce sentences that feel like they're coming like a deeply educated narrator, but after hours: "Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing."

Excerpt 1 fails more completely to capture this voice because it reaches for elevated language at the wrong times. "A whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury," "those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus," and "race, that insidious construct," sound like a narrator straining for erudition, instead of an erudite relaxing into confession.

Excerpt 2, by contrast, effectively conveys the tone of an academic in repose by combining elevated diction with conversational, almost oral constructions: "Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads)."
