Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: The Black Panther Party, a whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury, had been my crucible. I'd joined partly to prove a point, to silence the whispers that trailed me like a shadow. "Not Black enough," they hissed, both Black and white voices mingling in a chorus of disapproval. My crime? Muttering "Egads" during a heated basketball game, perhaps. Or maybe it was my novels, those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus, drawing accusations of elitism and worse, cultural betrayal. One particularly scathing review declared, "His Aeschylus is a betrayal of his Black heritage, a misguided attempt to elevate himself above his roots." The New York literary party, a swirling vortex of ambition and pretense, was no different. A literary agent, her eyes scanning the room for the next big thing, dismissed my work with a wave of her hand. "Forget Aeschylus," she scoffed, "write true, gritty real stories of Black life. That's what sells." I wanted to retort, "My life, my experience, isn't that Black enough for you?" But the words caught in my throat, choked by the weight of expectation. The agent, sensing my hesitation, moved on, her attention snagged by a performance artist reciting a monologue about the Black experience. The irony was thick enough to cut with a knife.  Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.

And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer?" From the original, "I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one." Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. written_by_Ashni.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.
written_by_Ashni.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_Ashni.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
written_by_Ashni.Reason: Option 1 is so uncharming – it flattens the voice, makes everything sound overly clean and self-conscious, and misses the original’s rhythm and bite. There’s no tension in it, no humor, no real sense of contradiction. It opens with a rhetorical question – “what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party?” – and proceeds to over-explain everything, draining it of the original’s brisk irony. Option 2 is much better: it captures the original’s dry wit, the frustration and performance around race, the absurdity of the literary world. The original notes: “I’ve heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused,” and Option 2 follows with a similar reviewer quote: “While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus’ Oresteia… seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience.” It also mirrors the performance-tinged New York party scene from the original with: “She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine.” It has voice in the right way – sharp, layered, self-aware.

written_by_James_Braun.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_James_Braun.Reason: Excerpt1 better fits the original. Like the original excerpt, is avoids purple imagery and maintains clear focus on what is proceeding in-scene. In contrast, paragraph2 is constantly employing similes that do not match the original tone ("Like a monk devoted …"; "like writing poetry at midnight"; etc.).

written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_Benjamin.Reason: The original excerpt is very meditative in nature, with an emphasis on the physical act of cooking and calming descriptions of the food, as seen in the line, "Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud." Excerpt 1 mirrors this style with phrases like "rich tomato-based (sauces) simmered for hours" and "the scent of sizzling garlic." Excerpt 2 veers away from the relaxing atmosphere that cooking creates and opens up ideas of loneliness, as in the line, "I imagined having guests to share my tea and salad." This interior/emotional description contrasts the original excerpt's focus on simply conveying action and leaving the narrator's feeling unexamined (" I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is").

It was a dish that demanded solitude, a quiet contemplation of the simple things in life. I had made a pilgrimage to a specialty store, a treasure trove of culinary tools, where I acquired a large pot, a gleaming stainless steel monument to my spaghetti ambitions, and a kitchen timer, its ticking a metronome marking the passage of time until my spaghetti was cooked to perfection.  From supermarkets catering to foreigners, I gathered exotic spices, plump tomatoes, and an assortment of pasta brands, each promising a unique spaghetti experience. My small apartment transformed into a spaghetti laboratory, filled with the rich aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, a fragrant symphony that clung to the curtains, the furniture, even my clothes. I experimented with countless sauces, each simmering on the stove, a testament to my dedication to the art of spaghetti. Sundays marked the beginning of my spaghetti week, a repetitive cycle of cooking and consuming spaghetti, my days revolving around this singular dish.  Tea and a simple salad were the supporting players, but spaghetti was the star, the center around which my culinary world revolved.  There was a comfort in this ritual, a sense of order in the twirling of the spaghetti, the methodical consumption of the dish.Spaghetti Days, I called them, stretching from Sunday to Sunday, a solitary symphony of flavors and textures, a testament to my love affair with this humble dish.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti. The process of cooking it was satisfying, but the idea of perfecting it was addictive. Like any dedicated student, I gathered the necessary equipment. I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original than Excerpt 2. Excerpt 1 shares this approach, mixing long sentences with shorter ones, and using lists of concrete images to create a vivid impression of the action ("My small apartment transformed into a spaghetti laboratory, filled with the rich aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, a fragrant symphony that clung to the curtains, the furniture, even my clothes"). written_by_Rachael.Original: My mother had a bachelor cousin a good deal younger than her, who used to visit us on the farm every summer. He brought along his mother, Aunt Nell Botts. His own name was Ernie Botts. He was a tall, florid man with a good-natured expression, a big square face, and fair curly hair springing straight up from his forehead. His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
written_by_Rachael.Reason: Excerpt1 feels slightly more in-line with the original excerpt. Excerpt2 takes too many liberties, to me, with how Ernie is portrayed. The specificity of his life as a school teacher, for instance, feels unlike the character in the original. Likewise, the narrator's position in relationship to him, especially her youthful mocking of him, feels off in paragraph2.

written_by_Yen.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts. Ernie. My younger cousin, who was to remain a lifelong bachelor, had once spent each summer with us on the farm, showing up shyly in tow that first season in the shadow of my Aunt Nell. I hadn’t liked having to share a room with my sister, as I did when he came to visit. But he made up for it, with his good-natured affability, and his curious habit of punctilious grooming. I’d had the idea to call him Earnest Bottom-and my use of this nickname behind his back brought my sister and myself no end of amusement. The visits stopped when Aunt Nell passed, Ernie then thirteen. His presence in our house dwindled to a card each Christmas in his spidery handwriting. At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life. That my cousin lived there too was the last thing on my mind. It was my mother who reminded me. She told me I should look him up, conjuring at once his easy, slightly high-pitched laugh, his perfectly brushed wool sweaters. From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. It wasn’t a cheap restaurant either, but one of those old-style, stiff tablecloth establishments that used to be in vogue then. We always had three courses and wine. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.
written_by_Yen.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—whom I privately called "Earnest Bottom" in those days of ruthless teenage cleverness—would arrive at our farm each summer with Aunt Nell, his clothes pressed and his hair neatly combed, as if the three-hour drive on dusty country roads had somehow failed to touch him. He had that particular quality of bachelor sons, a kind of pristine wholesomeness that spoke of carefully maintained routines and unspoken maternal guidance. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.
written_by_Yen.Reason:
Both paragraphs maintain a good degree of faithfulness to the author's straightforward style and the narrator's original reflections on class and family. Excerpt 1 has a stronger emphasis on the narrator's new and old lives in the city and country: "At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life". Where the original highlights class aspiration through "it probably cost more, strictly speaking than he could afford", Excerpt 2 deepens the speaker's reflections on Ernie and their family's class status through effective recollections and observations: "I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new." 

While it's a creative expansion, this part of Excerpt 2 remains firmly and naturally within the original's spirit of reminiscence, observation, and understated familial intimacy, cementing it as an overall better emulation.

written_by_Yen.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts. Ernie. My younger cousin, who was to remain a lifelong bachelor, had once spent each summer with us on the farm, showing up shyly in tow that first season in the shadow of my Aunt Nell. I hadn’t liked having to share a room with my sister, as I did when he came to visit. But he made up for it, with his good-natured affability, and his curious habit of punctilious grooming. I’d had the idea to call him Earnest Bottom-and my use of this nickname behind his back brought my sister and myself no end of amusement. The visits stopped when Aunt Nell passed, Ernie then thirteen. His presence in our house dwindled to a card each Christmas in his spidery handwriting. At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life. That my cousin lived there too was the last thing on my mind. It was my mother who reminded me. She told me I should look him up, conjuring at once his easy, slightly high-pitched laugh, his perfectly brushed wool sweaters. From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. It wasn’t a cheap restaurant either, but one of those old-style, stiff tablecloth establishments that used to be in vogue then. We always had three courses and wine. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.
written_by_Yen.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—whom I privately called "Earnest Bottom" in those days of ruthless teenage cleverness—would arrive at our farm each summer with Aunt Nell, his clothes pressed and his hair neatly combed, as if the three-hour drive on dusty country roads had somehow failed to touch him. He had that particular quality of bachelor sons, a kind of pristine wholesomeness that spoke of carefully maintained routines and unspoken maternal guidance. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: During those summers on the farm, Ernie Botts, who we’d mischievously dubbed “Earnest Bottom,” became a predictable part of the season, like the first crop of sweet corn or the relentless hum of cicadas. He was always impeccably groomed—his blond hair neatly combed, his fingernails somehow untouched by dirt, even after a day spent traipsing through the fields. He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: It is impossible to think of the Old Chelsea without thinking, too, of Earnest Bottom. His real name, of course, was Ernie Botts—my slightly younger and far more sophisticated cousin. We'd spent many summers together as children at my family's farm. Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.

written_by_Sophia.Original: When the shadow of the sash appeared on the curtains it was between seven and eight oclock and then I was in time again, hearing the watch. It was Grandfather’s and when Father gave it to me he said, Quentin, I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire; it’s rather excrutiatingly apt that you will use it to gain the reducto absurdum of all human experience which can fit your individual needs no better than it fitted his or his father’s. I give it to you not that you may remember time, but that you might forget it now and then for a moment and not spend all your breath trying to conquer it. Because no battle is ever won he said. They are not even fought. The field only reveals to man his own folly and despair, and victory is an illusion of philosophers and fools. It was propped against the collar box and I lay listening to it. Hearing it, that is. I dont suppose anybody ever deliberately listens to a watch or a clock. You dont have to. You can be oblivious to the sound for a long while, then in a second of ticking it can create in the mind unbroken the long diminishing parade of time you didn’t hear. Like Father said down the long and lonely light-rays you might see Jesus walking, like. And the good Saint Francis that said Little Sister Death, that never had a sister.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: Excerpt2 avoids the use of simile and metaphor that paragraph1 indulges ("like time itself across a curtain"; "across Sister Death herself"; "like that shadow, like that watch …"). For this reason, it better matches the tone of the original. Quinten's voice is erudite, but it is not overwrought or sweeping (paragraph2 is also guilty of this, but to a lesser degree, for me).

Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.

written_by_Benjamin.Original: When the shadow of the sash appeared on the curtains it was between seven and eight oclock and then I was in time again, hearing the watch. It was Grandfather’s and when Father gave it to me he said, Quentin, I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire; it’s rather excrutiatingly apt that you will use it to gain the reducto absurdum of all human experience which can fit your individual needs no better than it fitted his or his father’s. I give it to you not that you may remember time, but that you might forget it now and then for a moment and not spend all your breath trying to conquer it. Because no battle is ever won he said. They are not even fought. The field only reveals to man his own folly and despair, and victory is an illusion of philosophers and fools. It was propped against the collar box and I lay listening to it. Hearing it, that is. I dont suppose anybody ever deliberately listens to a watch or a clock. You dont have to. You can be oblivious to the sound for a long while, then in a second of ticking it can create in the mind unbroken the long diminishing parade of time you didn’t hear. Like Father said down the long and lonely light-rays you might see Jesus walking, like. And the good Saint Francis that said Little Sister Death, that never had a sister.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt1: The chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass hung cinched by the dark of the sash. It stood unstirred in the limpid bedroom air. No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age. My grandfather’s watch–which still belonged to my father even after his death as dogs belong to their buried owners, circling their grave and howling the premonitions my grandfather had uttered in his own bed: life being one big fever dream, all its hills and troughs in one fell swoop wrenched from under you, a dream from which you will be wrenched, and you wake in the unending dark where you take no triumphs with you, and the ceaseless hounds of timestamp flat your burial mound and the sky’s days pass beyond–ticked incessantly somewhere in the dark. My father talked about the dark in a similar night’s stifled room. How Saint Francis welcomed Little Sister Death as the dark all around Jesus when he walked along the long and lonely light-rays. Beyond that dark is nothing but dark, that we only know dark from the little light we got. We only know time because we count it, but countless time goes unticked in the unending dark, so much time there is no before, no after, the unnumbered breezes with no curtain to shape them. No, my time is never truly had. I felt the air too thick to breathe.
written_by_Benjamin.Excerpt2: The shadow of the sash falls down the curtain, a pallid crescent in the gloom of the room.  I can hear the ticking of the watch, a steady pulse in the quiet.  It was Grandfather’s watch, and now it is Father’s, and someday it will be mine.  The watch ticks on, a metronome marking the inexorable passage of time.  Father said, “You cannot conquer time.  You can only try to forget it.”  But how can one forget time when it is always there, ticking away, a constant reminder of our mortality?  The watch hands move, a slow, relentless dance towards the end.  “Time is a relentless and hungry force,” Father said.  “It devours all things – youth, beauty, even memory.”  The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives.  Each tick brings us closer to the end, to the final silence.  “Victories in life are fleeting,” Father said.  “They are but illusions in the face of time’s infinite and hungry maw.”  The watch ticks on, a constant reminder of our mortality.  It is a sound that haunts me, a sound that echoes the futility of our existence.  “Jesus walking on Galilee,” Father said, “and Saint Francis, speaking to his Little Sister Death.  Both of them knew that time could not be conquered, that it could only be endured.”  The watch ticks on, a steady beat in the silence of the room.  It is a sound that I cannot escape, a sound that reminds me of my own mortality.
written_by_Benjamin.Reason:
Excerpt 1 more closely resembles the original in both voice and style. The syntax is meandering and circuitous, and the language is philosophically dense, sometimes even abstract. The sentence “No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age,” destabilizes the reader and wraps the text in an obsessive quality; everything is alive, and everything is subject to time, it seems to tell us. In keeping with the original, Excerpt 1 allows language to disorient the reader but also offers moments of clarity we can anchor ourselves in, such as “we only know dark from the little light we got. We only know time because we count it”—which resonates with “They are not even fought. The field only reveals to man his own folly and despair”  in the original. 

Contrastingly, Excerpt 2 doesn't carry across the nuanced texture of the original’s language; instead, the tone is more declarative and less experimental. Sentences such as “The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives” or “a steady beat in the silence of the room” feel more expected and rehearsed than the communication of similar ideas in the original. For instance, the original excerpt’s statement: “I don't suppose anybody ever deliberately listens to a watch or a clock” gives the reader a sense that the narrator is realizing this as he writes it, making it more immediate and relatable.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.

written_by_Tian.Original: That was all. I knew then that if Margaret got me kicked out, it wouldn’t be for doing a thing as normal as sleeping with my master. And somehow, that disturbed me. I felt almost as though I really was doing something shameful, happily playing whore for my supposed owner. I went away feeling uncomfortable, vaguely ashamed.Time passed. Kevin and I became more a part of the household, familiar, accepted, accepting. That disturbed me too when I thought about it. How easily we seemed to acclimatize. Not that I wanted us to have trouble, but it seemed as though we should have had a harder time adjusting to this particular segment of history—adjusting to our places in the household of a slaveholder. For me, the work could be hard, but was usually more boring than physically wearing. And Kevin complained of boredom, and of having to be sociable with a steady stream of ignorant pretentious guests who visited the Weylin house. But for drop-ins from another century, I thought we had had a remarkably easy time. And I was perverse enough to be bothered by the ease.“This could be a great time to live in.”Kevin said once. “I keep thinking what an experience it would be to stay in it—go West and watch the building of the country, see how much of the Old West mythology is true.”“West,” I said bitterly. “That’s where they’re doing it to the Indians instead of the blacks!”
written_by_Tian.Excerpt1: After our fourth week on the plantation, what had begun as horrifying became mundane. The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. On a Friday afternoon, Kevin snuck by to make small talk. “I never thought I would see you folding napkins at a dining table.” What the hell was wrong with him? I seethed back, “Do you think I’m doing this for any other reason than my survival?” He replied, “Well, of course not. But I don’t exactly like going into town making social calls every which way as the master’s errand boy either.” Before I could interject to explain the mortal difference between indentured servitude and slavery, he went on to say, “We should escape, take advantage of this insanity, and see things people in our time dream of. I’ve always wondered what the real Wild West was like.” In the fields outside, I heard someone moan in pain. “The real West? This is the real West, Kevin. The fieldhand slaves outside generate the profits that the master reaps from the government. The government will use his raw goods to wipe out entire bloodlines of Lakota, Sioux, and countless other tribes. And in 200 years, white men will let their imaginations run wild in the lands their great-great-grandfathers slaughtered empty.
written_by_Tian.Excerpt2: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.

written_by_Harry.Excerpt1: The shame burned in my throat, a sour taste I couldn't swallow. Here I was, in this house, in this time, a part of this… this obscenity. Kevin beside me, and us both belonging to a man who thought us less than human.Margaret, with her sly smiles and knowing glances, she was a threat, I knew it. But not the normal kind, not the kind that would have Kevin bedding down with the master. No, this was something different, something more insidious.The days blurred, one into the next. The work, surprisingly, wasn't the hard part. It was the waiting, the knowing, the constant awareness of our place here. Kevin, bless his heart, seemed to find it all rather romantic. "Imagine," he'd say, his eyes alight, "exploring the West, seeing the cowboys and Indians."I'd just stare at him, the bile rising in my throat. "Cowboys and Indians," I'd scoff, "more like thieves and the stolen. While we're chained here in the South, they're out West taking land that never belonged to them."He'd frown, his romantic notions shattered. "It's not the same," he'd argue, "they're not slaves.""No," I'd retort, "but they're not free either. Not when their land is being taken, their way of life destroyed."He'd sigh, the conversation turning sour, as it always did. We were in this together, but we saw it so differently. He, with his head in the clouds, romanticizing the past. Me, with my feet on the ground, seeing the ugliness for what it was.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt2: My husband’s plan, while shame-inducing, worked. The master of the house believed I was Kevin’s slave, not his wife. I felt awkward around the house’s slaves. I’d tasted a freedom they would never see. Our only threat was Margaret, who seemed to notice that something was amiss. She could tell that we slept together, but a master taking a slave to bed was normal enough — Margaret was all too familiar with that. But perhaps she could tell that we didn’t belong in her era. We awaited that dangerous revelation for some time, but it never came. My work was bland, as was Kevin’s new social life. He always wanted a break despite never having to work. “I think, maybe,” he said, tossing an apple up and down as I cleaned, “we should get out of here. Explore. Visit the west? We could meet a real cowboy!” “So you suggest being nothing more than tourists? As my ancestors stay enslaved in the south? As the natives in the west are exploited?” I felt my voice shifting, becoming sharper, ready to stab. “We’ve traveled through time. Maybe we ought to change history.” Kevin contemplated my outburst, thoughtful but unemotional. “A tempting idea, but we shouldn’t interfere,” he said casually, bit into his apple, and left the room. I scrubbed away at the floor angrily. In this time, and even in our own, his life was made easier by history proceeding exactly as it had. Of course he didn’t want anything to change.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.

written_by_Connor.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day when I watched my mother die, though there was nothing lucky about that bitter-bright morning. The sun bounced off snow banks outside her window, creating a cruel sparkle that seemed to mock the dimming light within. A cup of green Jell-O sat untouched on her bedside table – some nurse's attempt at festivity that now seemed obscene in its cheerfulness. My mother's eyes were the color of forgotten summers, a blue so startling against her pallid skin that it made my chest ache. They remained open, fixed on something I couldn't see, something beyond the sterile hospital walls and my desperate presence beside her. I watched death move through her like smoke through a burning house, slow and inevitable, claiming each room until nothing remained but ash. Those eyes – I saw everything in them. First came the bitterness, sharp as broken glass, then confusion that softened her face into something childlike, and finally, a quiet courage that broke my heart and rebuilt it in the same moment. The blue of her irises burned like pilot lights, struggling to stay lit even as the rest of her failed. Even now, I can close my eyes and see that color, that last fierce flag of life she waved, refusing to surrender until the very end. How wild it was, to watch someone both fight and accept their fate in the same endless moment.
written_by_Connor.Excerpt2: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?

written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray.  I sat beside her bed, the green Jell-O untouched on the bedside table, a festive offering she couldn’t partake in.  Outside, the snow was falling, the last of winter’s icy grip, the sunlight reflecting off the white expanse in a dazzling display.  But in this room, there was a different kind of dimming, a slow, inevitable burning down to smoke.She wasn’t asleep, not quite, but somewhere between here and there, her breath shallow, her body still.  Yet, her eyes, those strikingly blue eyes, remained open, vivid against the pale skin, the stark white sheets.  It was in those eyes that I saw it all unfold – the bitterness that had clung to her like a shroud, the bewilderment at the body’s betrayal, and then, finally, a quiet heroism.  The blue, so vibrant, so alive, was a defiance, a refusal to let go, even as the current pulled her away.I watched her, my mother, her spirit flickering like a candle flame in the gathering darkness.  And in those blue depths, I saw the echo of the life she had lived, the love she had given, the strength she had shown.  It was a story written in the language of the heart, a story that would live on, even as the last embers of her life faded away.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.

written_by_Rachael.Original: "The only reason you say that race was not an issue is because you wish it was not. We all wish it was not. But it’s a lie. I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America. When you are black in America and you fall in love with a white person, race doesn’t matter when you’re alone together because it’s just you and your love. But the minute you step outside, race matters. But we don’t talk about it. We don’t even tell our white partners the small things that piss us off and the things we wish they understood better, because we’re worried they will say we’re overreacting, or we’re being too sensitive. And we don’t want them to say, Look how far we’ve come, just forty years ago it would have been illegal for us to even be a couple blah blah blah, because you know what we’re thinking when they say that? We’re thinking why the fuck should it ever have been illegal anyway? But we don’t say any of this stuff. We let it pile up inside our heads and when we come to nice liberal dinners like this, we say that race doesn’t matter because that’s what we’re supposed to say, to keep our nice liberal friends comfortable. It’s true. I speak from experience." The host, a Frenchwoman, glanced at her American husband, a slyly pleased smile on her face; the most unforgettable dinner parties happened when guests said unexpected, and potentially offensive, things.The poet shook her head and said to the host, “I’d love to take some of that wonderful dip home if you have any left,” and looked at the others as though she could not believe they were actually listening to Ifemelu. But they were, all of them hushed, their eyes on Ifemelu as though she was about to give up a salacious secret that would both titillate and implicate them. Ifemelu had been drinking too much white wine; from time to time she had a swimming sensation in her head, and she would later send apology e-mails to the host and the poet. But everyone was watching her, even Blaine, whose expression she could not, for once, read clearly. And so she began to talk about Curt.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt1: "It's amazing, how the same things that happen between a man and a woman can be so different simply because of their race." She paused, swirling the wine in her glass, the crystal catching the light. "Before I came here, I never really thought of myself as Black." The table, a mix of faces, both familiar and new, leaned in, intrigued. "But here, suddenly, I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm a Black woman dating a white man." She let out a small, humorless laugh. "It's like this whole other layer gets added, this… awareness, this constant hum in the background that you can't quite ignore." "But things are so much better now, no?" The Frenchwoman, her accent a delicate lilt, tilted her head. "You couldn't even… you know…" she trailed off, gesturing vaguely. "Marry each other?" She finished for her, feeling the familiar sting. "Yes, we've 'progressed.' Now we can be together, but we still have to tiptoe around all the unspoken things." She took another sip, the wine warming her throat, loosening her tongue. "Like, I can't get too angry, can't disagree too strongly, because then I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm the angry Black woman." "Oh, but that's…" the poet, his brow furrowed, shifted uncomfortably. "I mean, surely, it's not…" "Food's getting cold, don't you think?" Blaine, ever the diplomat, interjected smoothly. But she was on a roll, the words tumbling out, fueled by the wine and years of unspoken frustrations. "And it's not just him, it's everyone. This constant… need to remind me how far we've come. As if I should be grateful." She looked around the table, their faces a mixture of fascination and discomfort. "You know, 'Remember when you couldn't even have a drink at the same bar?' As if that somehow makes everything okay now." "But…" the poet started, but she cut him off. "It's like this weird performance, you know? Always being aware of how I'm perceived, what I represent." She met Blaine's eyes across the table, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, I want to… scream, to break free from this invisible script that everyone seems to have for me." A heavy silence settled over the table. She knew she was oversharing, knew she'd regret this in the morning. But tonight, the wine had given her a voice, a raw, unfiltered voice. "Like with Curt, for example…" she began, feeling a new wave of memories, a new wave of honesty, washing over her.
written_by_Rachael.Excerpt2: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! She paused, swirling the wine in her glass, the crystal catching the light. "Before I came here, I never really thought of myself as Black." The original author tends to have a very direct style and the main character’s speech is usually distinguished by lots of strong declarative sentences. This is better captured in P2, where the author uses exclamation points and no ellipses. Like the original, E2 doesn’t waste any time on these decorative visual descriptions – every sentence further characterizes the tension between Ifemelu and her fellow dinner guests.
