written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.
written_by_Cara.Reason: P1 is more similar to the Original than P2. It operates in a more summaritive way than P2, similar to the Original, whereas E2 feels much more grounded in scene (For example, a French woman in E2 directly asks the question about 50 years of progress, whereas in the original it is recounted in monologue by Ifemelu). E1 in general operates in a monologue style that feels more similar to the Original, with Ifemelu's dialogue taking up most of the focus and pagespace of the paragraph. E1 and the Original also feel more general and less particular in its argument, whereas the argument in E2 is more specific and personal, and contains more figurative language "[Racism] is pressing against your throat," "Race in America is like the weather," etc.

written_by_Cara.Original: "The only reason you say that race was not an issue is because you wish it was not. We all wish it was not. But it’s a lie. I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America. When you are black in America and you fall in love with a white person, race doesn’t matter when you’re alone together because it’s just you and your love. But the minute you step outside, race matters. But we don’t talk about it. We don’t even tell our white partners the small things that piss us off and the things we wish they understood better, because we’re worried they will say we’re overreacting, or we’re being too sensitive. And we don’t want them to say, Look how far we’ve come, just forty years ago it would have been illegal for us to even be a couple blah blah blah, because you know what we’re thinking when they say that? We’re thinking why the fuck should it ever have been illegal anyway? But we don’t say any of this stuff. We let it pile up inside our heads and when we come to nice liberal dinners like this, we say that race doesn’t matter because that’s what we’re supposed to say, to keep our nice liberal friends comfortable. It’s true. I speak from experience." The host, a Frenchwoman, glanced at her American husband, a slyly pleased smile on her face; the most unforgettable dinner parties happened when guests said unexpected, and potentially offensive, things.The poet shook her head and said to the host, “I’d love to take some of that wonderful dip home if you have any left,” and looked at the others as though she could not believe they were actually listening to Ifemelu. But they were, all of them hushed, their eyes on Ifemelu as though she was about to give up a salacious secret that would both titillate and implicate them. Ifemelu had been drinking too much white wine; from time to time she had a swimming sensation in her head, and she would later send apology e-mails to the host and the poet. But everyone was watching her, even Blaine, whose expression she could not, for once, read clearly. And so she began to talk about Curt.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt1: Ifemelu took another sip of her chardonnay. She knew she should let the subject drop, but the wine was giving her a slight buzz that made her feel emboldened, and she suddenly felt they all needed to hear what she had to say. "Racism is nowhere near over in America," she said, "despite what we may tell our white friends and lovers because we don't want to make them feel uncomfortable." She gestured with her wine glass, pointing at her hosts, then at herself. "The truth is, I've never been more aware that I'm Black than I have been since coming to America. In Nigeria, I hardly thought of my race. But here, I'm constantly reminded of it, and not just by racists and rednecks like you might think, but by white liberals, academics, even other Black people, to tell you the truth. And to make matters worse, I can't say anything about it, or I'll be seen as making a fuss since we've apparently come so far. They'll point out that I have a white boyfriend and no one gives me any trouble for it, when interracial marriage used to be illegal. They call that progress when that's the bare minimum. Frankly, it's patronizing." Ifemelu looked pointedly at the poet, who had kept her head down and was picking at her salad. The poet avoided her eye contact and instead turned to the hostess, as if she sensed an opportunity to change the subject. "This salad is so delicious," she said, holding up a forkful of greens. The hostess thanked her, but she was still watching Ifemelu with anticipation and maybe some detached amusement, since this wasn't her home country, and Ifemelu had said nothing about France. Her American husband, meanwhile, seemed excited to have his cadre of polite and well-educated liberals challenged by this unfamiliar woman, his friend's new girlfriend. Ifemelu reached for the wine glass again and looked up at Blaine to see if she'd gone too far, but his gaze was inscrutable, though fixed on her. Well, if what he loved about me is my mind, he can't be mad if I speak it, she thought. And if she said something too scandalous, she could always write them an apology note later. And before she could stop herself, she was telling them all the deeply personal stuff about her struggles while dating Curt.
written_by_Cara.Excerpt2:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."

written_by_James_Braun.Original: Your girl catches you cheating. (Well, actually she’s your fiancée, but hey, in a bit it so won’t matter.) She could have caught you with one sucia, she could have caught you with two, but because you’re a totally batshit cuero who never empties his e-mail trash can, she caught you with fifty! Sure, over a six-year period, but still. Fifty fucking girls? God damn! Maybe if you’d been engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita you could have survived it—but you’re not engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita. Your girl is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn’t believe in open anything; in fact, the one thing she warned you about, that she swore she would never forgive, was cheating. I’ll put a machete in you, she promised. And, of course, you swore you wouldn’t do it. You swore you wouldn’t. You swore you wouldn’t.And you did.She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time. Because you’ve gone through so much together—her father’s death, your tenure madness, her bar exam (passed on the third attempt). And because love, real love, is not so easily shed. written_by_Sean_Cavanaugh.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.
written_by_Sean_Cavanaugh.Reason: Excerpt2 is closer to the original excerpt. Excerpt1 is too exaggerated in its attempt to replicate the narratorial voice and use of slang ("Well, cue the platano peel, because homie, you slipped. Fifty fucking girls. Once a year that’s half a siglo."; "Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae."; etc.). Actually, you find out it’s chill. At least for a few months. Steady as it goes." vs. "You swore you wouldn’t. And you did. She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time." in the original). I also prefer the way paragraph2 grounds itself in scenes ("You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too." or "That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come"). While I prefer the ending deadpan of paragraph1 in some senses, it feels unapologetic and so does not match the tone of the original.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.
written_by_Sophia.Reason: The figurative language in the first excerpt more closely mirrors the original -- it captures the feeling of inevitability that is evoked in the original ("like the snow, we continued to die"): "creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm." Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community ..." (The correlation between "snapping jaws" and "unraveling" doesn't quite work here.) The formal language at the end of excerpt two also breaks with the tone of the original excerpt; p2 suddenly stops employing naturalistic metaphors and veers into an overt sentimentality/over-explanation that's not found in the original or in p1: "Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp ... [The government] seek[s] more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity."

For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.

While both paragraphs are effective and well-written, each misses a key component of the original. The original monologue's central qualities are its emphasis on the active, human relationships --- even violent --- with the surrounding fauna, "I guided the last buffalo hunt. Furthermore, it adds a heroism to the ending with "daring them to try harder, without fear" that discounts the totality of the genocide described here. 

Overall, Excerpt 1's absences are less conspicuous, and it avoids the ethical pitfalls of Excerpt 2, ultimately better emulating the emotional beats of the original monologue.

written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Original: The day that Junior fell down began like any other day: the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges, the prayer chants in the distance, the cheap film music rising from the floor below, the loud pelvic thrusts of an 'item number' dancing across a neighbor’s TV, a child’s cry, a mother’s rebuke, unexplained laughter, scarlet expectorations, bicycles, the newly plaited hair of schoolgirls, the smell of strong sweet coffee, a green wing flashing in a tree. Senior and Junior, two very old men, opened their eyes in their bedrooms on the fourth floor of a sea-green building on a leafy lane, just out of sight of Elliot’s Beach, where, that evening, the young would congregate, as they always did, to perform the rites of youth, not far from the village of the fisherfolk, who had no time for such frivolity. The poor were puritans by night and day. As for the old, they had rites of their own and did not need to wait for evening. With the sun stabbing at them through their window blinds, the two old men struggled to their feet and lurched out onto their adjacent verandas, emerging at almost the same moment, like characters in an ancient tale, trapped in fateful coincidences, unable to escape the consequences of chance.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt1: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Excerpt2: The sun, a molten fist, clenched the city in its fiery grip, the heat so ferocious it could melt the wings of sparrows foolish enough to take flight.  The air, thick with the chanting of prayers from nearby temples and the tinny melodies of Hindi film songs, crackled with the cries of children playing cricket in dusty alleyways.  The aroma of freshly brewed coffee, dark and bitter, snaked through the streets, mingling with the pungent scent of spices from open-air markets.On the fourth floor of a sea-green building, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, stirred in their beds, their bodies attuned to the city's relentless rhythm.  As if bound by an invisible thread, they woke up at precisely the same moment, their eyes fluttering open in unison.  They stepped out onto their respective verandas, their movements slow and deliberate, a stark contrast to the frenetic energy of the streets below. Downstairs, the younger generation buzzed with anticipation, their voices a chorus of excitement as they planned their evening escapades at Elliot's Beach.  But the old men remained unfazed, their world a sanctuary of quietude amidst the chaos.  Senior gazed at the distant sea, its shimmering surface mirroring the turmoil within his own soul.  Junior, his eyes fixed on the horizon, seemed lost in a reverie, the past and present blurring in his mind's eye
written_by_Adesuwa_Agbonile.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original than Excerpt 2; like the original, which lists the different sounds and sights that characterize the morning ("the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges," etc.), Excerpt 1 begins with a panoramic view of the morning's activities, like "he children were already awake and fussing for food" and "Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee," whereas Excerpt 2 foregoes the list and instead uses long sentences, with lots of adverbs and adjectives, to undertake this world-building exercise ("The sun, a molten fist" and "The air, thick with the chanting"). Excerpt 1 also presents the coincidence between Junior and Senior's morning routines in a more succinct and straightforward manner than Excerpt 2, which moves slower and presents this coincidence, again, through a long sentence with figurative language ("As if bound by an invisible thread, they woke up at precisely the same moment, their eyes fluttering open in unison.")

written_by_Sophia.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. My mother told him this. “Your work,” she said. “You’ve been writing about the Bible.” He nodded, as if this was something he could accept, though not something he quite believed. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: My father, a stranger in his own house, sits hunched in his armchair, a shadow of the man I knew.  His eyes, once bright and full of life, are now clouded with confusion.  He struggles to remember what he's working on, a question met with a sigh and a shake of his head.  My mother, her face etched with worry, reminds him gently, "Your writing, dear, on the Bible and anti-Semitism."  A flicker of recognition crosses his face, a brief spark in the fading embers of his mind.He looks at me, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.  "My daughter," he says, his voice a fragile whisper, "so proud of you."  But the light fades quickly, replaced by a vacant stare.  "Nothing to say," he murmurs, lost in the labyrinth of his own thoughts.  The silence that follows is heavy, filled with unspoken words and a growing sense of loss.Later, my mother shows me a photograph from forty years ago.  My father, young and vibrant, stands with his arm around her, both of them radiating joy.  My mother's voice cracks as she speaks, her words laced with a quiet despair.  "It's like he's already gone," she says, her eyes filled with tears.  I look at the photograph again, the image of my father frozen in time, a stark contrast to the frail figure sitting in the other room.  The weight of his absence, even in his presence, settles over me, a heavy cloak of sorrow that I cannot shake off.

written_by_Sara.Excerpt1: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."
written_by_Sara.Excerpt2: I visit my father and immediately notice new changes. The way he holds his coffee cup with both hands now, like a child. The way his eyes move around the room without settling. When I ask about his work, he stares at the wall behind me. My mother quickly fills the silence: "Tell her about your writing on the Bible, dear. The anti-Semitism research." He nods, but I can see he's already forgotten the prompt. "I'm proud of you," he says to me suddenly, then adds, "though I have nothing to say." I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance. Later, my mother pulls me aside to show me a photograph. "Look," she says, "this was forty years ago." In it, my father stands straight-backed beside a podium, papers spread before him like fallen leaves. I notice how his collar sits perfectly against his neck, how his hands rest purposefully on the wooden edge. My mother's fingers tremble slightly as she returns the photo to its drawer. I think: This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.
written_by_Sara.Reason: Both of these are pretty good but I prefer P2. In P1, the narrator reveals some additional emotional layers that are not present in the original and therefore change the tone significantly – “I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot” and “I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl”. The author of E2 is more detached, describing the painful events in a matter-of-fact way, which is closer to the original. There are some personal asides - “ I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance.” - but they are less dramatic and more consistent with the original author’s voice.

written_by_Sara.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.

written_by_Devin.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”
written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world.  My gaze drifted back to my plate, the food suddenly as bland as the pity I felt for myself.  Later, my father's voice, rough with suppressed resentment, dissected the meal, the "pig slop" mashed potatoes becoming a metaphor for our diminished status.  We were not "à la carte" patrons, and our presence was a mere tolerated intrusion.  The restaurant, a microcosm of society, had laid bare the invisible lines that defined our place.
written_by_Devin.Excerpt2: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
written_by_Devin.Reason: Excerpt 2 is closer to the original than Excerpt 1. Excerpt 2, like the original, is composed of short, descriptive sentences that make sparing use of adverbs and adjectives. In the original, the opening sentence conveys both the opulence of the restaurant and the discomfort of the characters at once: "One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele." Excerpt 2 achieves the same understated yet clear tone of voice, albeit over the course of two sentences: "My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food." Meanwhile, Excerpt 1 attempts the same effect, but rather than employing a subtler approach, it veers toward melodrama and overwriting: "In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement." Excerpt 2, like the original, also presents the narrator's self-portrait, in comparison to the young girl dining beside him: "Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time." Excerpt 1 foregoes this, and so departs from the original.

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. My father's hands, roughened by work, rested uneasily on the paper placemat while we waited, ignored by the waiters who glided past with studied indifference. At the next table, a girl my age lounged with casual elegance, her summer-bronzed skin gleaming against a crisp white blouse. She spooned yogurt—a food I had never tasted—with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence. Her father, well-dressed and at ease, gestured expressively as he spoke to her. They had ordered à la carte, their plates arranged with careful precision by attentive staff. When our fixed-price meals finally arrived, the mashed potatoes sat in a grayish heap, unmolded from some industrial container. My father ate in silence, his shoulders tense, his fork scraping the institutional plate. For days afterward, he would mutter about the "pig slop" they had served us, each repetition of the phrase carrying the accumulated weight of a lifetime of similar humiliations. I understood then that the restaurant had sorted us, placed us in our proper social category—the cheap seats, the hurried service, the institutional food. We belonged to the world of fixed-price menus and group tables, while others inhabited the realm of individual choice, of yogurt and carefully plated dishes, of being seen and served with deference.
written_by_James_Cato.Reason: Option 2 is stronger. It captures more of the original’s clarity and sociological precision. The details are well observed, and the voice holds that careful tension between seeing and not yet fully understanding. The original says: “I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad- looking… I could see everything that separated me from that girl.” Option 2 mirrors that dissonance: “My spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn,” contrasted with “a girl… her summer-bronzed skin gleaming… spooned yogurt… with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence.” Option 1 pushes too hard and feels less grounded. Lines like “my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics” are more stylized than the moment calls for. Option 2 better conveys the original's quiet ache and the slow understanding of being out of place.

written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. written_by_Renne_Flory.Original: Before the flight I was invited for lunch at a London club with a billionaire I’d been promised had liberal credentials. He talked in his open-necked shirt about the new software he was developing, that could help organisations identify the employees most likely to rob and betray them in the future. We were meant to be discussing a literary magazine he was thinking of starting up: unfortunately I had to leave before we arrived at that subject. He insisted on paying for a taxi to the airport, which was useful since I was late and had a heavy suitcase.The billionaire had been keen to give me the outline of his life story, which had begun unprepossessingly and ended – obviously – with him being the relaxed, well-heeled man who sat across the table from me today. I wondered whether in fact what he wanted now was to be a writer, with the literary magazine as his entrée. A lot of people want to be writers: there was no reason to think you couldn’t buy your way into it. This man had bought himself in, and out, of a great many things. He mentioned a scheme he was working on, to eradicate lawyers from people’s personal lives. He was also developing a blueprint for a floating wind farm big enough to accommodate the entire community of people needed to service and run it: the gigantic platform could be located far out to sea, thus removing the unsightly turbines from the stretch of coast where he was hoping to pilot the proposal and where, incidentally, he owned a house. On Sundays he played drums in a rock band, just for fun. He was expecting his eleventh child, which wasn’t as bad as it sounded when you considered that he and his wife had once adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. I was finding it difficult to assimilate everything I was being told. The waitresses kept bringing more things, oysters, relishes, special wines. He was easily distracted, like a child with too many Christmas presents. But when he put me in the taxi he said, enjoy yourself in Athens, though I didn’t remember telling him that was where I was going.

Everyone wants to write, I’ve noticed; everyone imagines themselves a writer, even if they have never put pen to paper. The billionaire had funded a good many ambitious ventures. A floating wind farm with worker houses, and something about a scheme to eliminate lawyers for managing personal matters. The waitress came along with another round of drinks. A perfect cube of ice sat in the center of each. I was struggling to process most of what the billionaire had said, the dishes before us becoming more and more luxurious, and expensive. His frenetic, scattered storytelling and sweet enthusiasm felt childlike against the opulence of our experience, of this lunch. When he put me in my taxi, he said ‘Enjoy yourself in Athens.’ This surprised me, as I didn’t recall telling him my destination. Actually I could not remember saying anything during our lunch.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: The club's mahogany-paneled dining room felt both intimate and imposing, much like the billionaire himself who sat across from me in his unexpectedly casual attire - a contradiction that seemed to epitomize the entire encounter. He spoke of his software project with the same blithe enthusiasm one might discuss a hobby, though its purpose - to predict employee betrayal - carried an unmistakable darkness beneath its technological sheen. I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?

written_by_Patrick.Original: It takes Kant a year to write the one-paragraph mass email, another three weeks to compile the Coming Out mailing list of friends, family, and colleagues, and three bourbons to actually send it. For his entire life he has so grotesquely imagined the consequences of public exposure that he’s only recently, at thirty-one, stopped hedging to himself that he is bi or “flexible.” He pictures his mother saying she never wants to speak to him again; he imagines dying alone in an unheated tenement, though he knows this is unlikely to happen to a video-game asset designer with two degrees. Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.
written_by_Patrick.Excerpt1: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_Patrick.Excerpt2: Kant's coming out email sat in his drafts folder like a grenade with the pin half-pulled, while he spent weeks A/B testing subject lines, as if the right combination of words could defuse three decades of queerness into something digestible for his mother's WeChat circles. He'd crafted seventeen versions, each more baroque than the last, padding them with disclaimers and preemptive responses to imagined objections, until the final draft read like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation. The responses, when they finally came, were an anticlimactic parade of heart emojis and "love you no matter what"s—the kind of tepid acceptance that made him wonder if perhaps he wasn't gay enough to warrant proper drama. His coworkers replied with the practiced neutrality of people who'd attended exactly one diversity training, while his mother's response ("Ok. Did you eat dinner?") felt like being handed a participation trophy for surviving thirty-one years of internal torment. He'd prepared for scorched earth but got lukewarm validation, and now here he was, somehow lonelier in his freedom, spending his newly authentic life watching YouTube compilations of gay wedding flash mobs and ordering rainbow-colored socks he'd never wear. The Year of Damp Feet, he called it in his journal, though he knew the phrase would sound better in someone else's memoir. His therapist called this "adjustment period" progress, but it felt more like trading one closet for another—this one just happened to have better lighting and an Amazon Prime subscription. The truth was, he'd gotten good at being afraid, had built his personality around it like a pearl around grit, and now that the fear was gone, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he'd peaked at being closeted, that he'd somehow gentrified his own identity into something too palatable to matter, too sanitized for the revolution he'd imagined himself starring in.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: For seven months, thirty-one-year old Kant tried to come out. He had decided that the most optimized method would take the form of mass email, as text could be perfected, and, in these many months, perfected the text: it was nearly a work of art, forthcoming without oversharing (he’d received feedback from internet forums), and grammar checked. It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. By the time that he’d finished the anxious rigamarole, a few replies had come in, and the reality became obvious: he’d been received with open-arms and heart emojis. His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. In the days after he’d sent the email, he didn’t feel compelled to download any apps or sit at a stool in the gay bar down the street. A part of him wished for adversity, or at least the accompanying opportunity to rise above it, but he was left with an understanding that nothing had changed, that declaration didn’t always inspire action. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: Kant, a connoisseur of solitude, had always envisioned his coming-out as a cataclysmic event, a meteor strike that would leave a crater in his life.  He'd spent weeks crafting the perfect email, a digital dove carrying the olive branch of his truth.  His imagination, a master of disaster, painted vivid scenes of his mother's tearful rejection, his friends recoiling in horror, and his colleagues whispering behind his back.But reality, it turned out, was a terrible painter.  The email launched, and instead of a meteor shower, there was a gentle rain of heart emojis from friends, muted acknowledgments from coworkers, and a carefully worded acceptance from his parents.  No drama, no disinheritance, not even a decent argument. Kant was baffled.  Where was the transformative growth?  The epic struggle he had envisioned himself overcoming?  Instead of relief, he felt a perverse disappointment, a sense of anticlimax that left him feeling strangely unfulfilled.His post-coming-out life was marked by inertia, an endless parade of solitary evenings and damp socks.  He'd walk home alone, his footsteps echoing in the cavernous silence of his apartment, the air thick with the scent of unwashed laundry and existential loneliness.He'd spend hours on the internet, scrolling through endless feeds of other people's curated lives, each post a tiny dagger to his heart.  He'd watch reality TV, the inane chatter of the contestants a poor substitute for human connection. He'd even tried dating, but his heart wasn't in it.  Each date felt like a performance, a carefully choreographed dance of small talk and forced smiles.  He'd find himself longing for the solitude of his apartment, the comforting embrace of his damp socks. Kant's year of damp feet was a testament to the enduring power of fear, a fear that had not only kept him closeted for years but had also robbed him of the joy of his own liberation.  He was free, but he was alone, a prisoner of his own making.
