written_by_Harry.Original: “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Please contact the pharmacy immediately.” The announcement played again, but Dr. Y was apparently still missing.The elevator was crowded with doctors and nurses, and patients with drip bags of yellow liquid, but I forced my way in and pressed the button for the sixth floor. I was sure I’d be able to find her room. I would pretend I was just visiting her, or I could say I wanted her to pay me for the bag. After all, I ought to get something for all my work.First, I’ll apologize for the other day—very humbly, in order to regain her trust. And then I’ll say what I’ve come to say: “Making your bag has been a very important experience for me. I don’t think I’ll ever have the chance to make a piece like this again. Still, I’m happy you’re getting the operation and won’t need the bag. But I do have one final request: I’d like to see it put to its intended use just once. I know it’s asking a lot, but I’d be very grateful. I promise I’ll never bother you again, but nothing is more painful for a craftsman than knowing all his hard work was for nothing. Just this once, and I’d be eternally grateful.”She’ll take off her gown, and I’ll fit it on her.“Are you satisfied, then?” she’ll ask, eager to be rid of me.“Thank you,” I’ll say, but when I reach for the bag, I’ll cut her heart away, too.And then it will be mine alone.The bag is in my left pocket. I tried to fold it flat, but there’s a little mound in my pants. I don’t think anyone will notice. The shears in my right pocket prick my thigh as I wait.The elevator chimes, the number six lights up, and the door opens.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt1: As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still. The voice over the intercom announced, “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to ward three,” in a steady monotone, a voice unbothered by the frantic shuffle of nurses and patients around me. The air was tinged with a faint medicinal scent, sharp and sterile, as though the building itself exhaled nothing but clean, cold breath. My thoughts drifted toward her, lying somewhere beyond these walls, fragile and unguarded.The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand. I imagined the look in her eyes as I approached, a flicker of recognition perhaps, then the inevitable softening—a crack in the shield of suspicion she might have built around herself. My words were carefully chosen in advance, rehearsed in the quiet moments of the previous night: admiration for her grace, a humble explanation of my creation, a plea for forgiveness wrapped in layers of calm sincerity.And yet, the weight of the shears burned against the lining of the bag, a cold promise of something darker. The thought of her chest rising and falling, her heart pulsing rhythmically beneath the soft fabric of her gown, stirred a sensation I couldn’t quite place. My grip on the strap tightened as the fantasy took shape—a vision of my hands steady, precise, separating her from the fragile organ that held her life. The bag would hold it perfectly, as it was meant to.The elevator dinged, and the doors slid open to reveal the sixth floor. The hall stretched out before me, fluorescent lights reflecting off the polished floors. I stepped out, the bag heavy in my hand, and began walking toward her room.
written_by_Harry.Excerpt2: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.

written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.

I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.

Please contact the pharmacy immediately.” The announcement played again, but Dr. Y was apparently still missing.The elevator was crowded with doctors and nurses, and patients with drip bags of yellow liquid, but I forced my way in and pressed the button for the sixth floor. I was sure I’d be able to find her room. I would pretend I was just visiting her, or I could say I wanted her to pay me for the bag. After all, I ought to get something for all my work.First, I’ll apologize for the other day—very humbly, in order to regain her trust. And then I’ll say what I’ve come to say: “Making your bag has been a very important experience for me. I don’t think I’ll ever have the chance to make a piece like this again. Still, I’m happy you’re getting the operation and won’t need the bag. But I do have one final request: I’d like to see it put to its intended use just once. I know it’s asking a lot, but I’d be very grateful. I promise I’ll never bother you again, but nothing is more painful for a craftsman than knowing all his hard work was for nothing. Just this once, and I’d be eternally grateful.”She’ll take off her gown, and I’ll fit it on her.“Are you satisfied, then?” she’ll ask, eager to be rid of me.“Thank you,” I’ll say, but when I reach for the bag, I’ll cut her heart away, too.And then it will be mine alone.The bag is in my left pocket. I tried to fold it flat, but there’s a little mound in my pants. I don’t think anyone will notice. The shears in my right pocket prick my thigh as I wait.The elevator chimes, the number six lights up, and the door opens.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt1: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. A young doctor in a white coat pressed against the back wall, studying a clipboard, while two nurses whispered near the buttons, their voices barely audible above the mechanical hum. The speakers crackled: "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to Ward 3." I watched the numbers illuminate one by one: three, four, five. The bag I had made was perfect—every stitch aligned with precision, the leather supple and warm like living skin. I had spent weeks crafting it, imagining her face when she would first hold it, how her fingers would trace the seams I had sewn with such care. Now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose, like the shears tucked carefully in my coat pocket. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.
written_by_Caroline_Waring.Excerpt2: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.

written_by_Stefan.Original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt1: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
written_by_Stefan.Excerpt2: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_Stefan.Reason: Both the original and second excerpt use precise details to evoke the way that the resort once was, in stark contrast to how Africans/Africa recently repurposed the resort ("Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in ... to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut" in original; "But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth" in p2). The first excerpt, when it uses precise images and details, paints a vague portrait of abandon, without this idea that this is "Africanness" reasserting itself: "But there were still definite traces of life—beetles ..., vines ..., thickets of brush with twig-like branches." The idea that the resort is not for tourists but rather a makeshift version of Europe is also present in p2 and the original, illustrated by the precise details of how the resort once functioned: "It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt1: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: The once-vibrant resort now stood in a state of decay, a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region.  The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original because it has a subtler approach to the subject matter than Excerpt 2. While Excerpt 2 directly addresses the "societal shifts" and "the complexities of post-colonial identity," Excerpt 1 focuses on imagery and descriptions that conjure the setting's atmosphere---a strategy more aligned with the style of the original. The details given in Excerpt 1 also have greater specificity, which more closely echoes the imagery of the original.

written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.

The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Once gleaming and luxurious, the resort now tells stories of upheaval in every ballroom and courtyard. This resort of yesterday fares poorly today, and no one comes. Beige African sidewalks collect debris, chairs in the European style and English books. A discarded packet of Belga cigarettes transports visitors to another time, allowing them to trespass on the resort in its antebellum years. The whole discarded era becomes visible—Europeans on holiday attempting to make a home of another's home. Visitors may traipse through the relics spilling from sidewalk to grass, walking on both. Now it is a place hung between that past and a present that has not shaken what came before. Children from town tell stories about the resort, what it was and what lives there now: ghosts of both the travelers and the locals who worked in the lobbies and kitchens when the building retained its purpose, ghosts in luxury clothing inappropriate for the climate and ghosts in neatly pressed uniforms. The older teens climb inside through gaps in the boarded windows and explore the detritus, daring each other to venture deeper and deeper down unlit hallways smelling of mold and dust. They speak in whispers. This small entertainment is laced with the petty danger that emanates now from the building. It can be called a harmless thing, a relic of before: before the departures of the whites and the Asians, before independence, before the mutinies. Yet the building, an ugly shell of itself, persists. It says: "But here I still am."
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: The resort bore the weight of its past in every crumbling façade and every shattered tile strewn across the once-immaculate promenade. The sidewalks were now a repository for the discarded detritus of another era—splintered furniture, faded paperbacks, and Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot, their familiar logo a ghostly reminder of European elegance. The air, still humid and heavy, carried a vague scent of salt and mildew, mingled with the decay of abandonment. Here, the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow over the resort's decline. Once a haven for settlers who sought to conjure a slice of Europe amidst Africa's heat, it now stood as a relic of disillusionment. The verandas where drinks had clinked under the laughter of expatriates were hollow, their railings stripped of paint, exposing a rusted skeleton beneath.The tide of independence had washed away the veneer of its purpose. Military mutinies had marked its walls with bullet scars; the exodus of the white and Asian populations had left its rooms unclaimed, their emptiness profound. The palm trees swayed in the wind, their silhouettes etched against a bruised sky, but even they seemed tired, their leaves curling at the edges like burnt paper. What once exuded vitality now lay inert, a tableau of exile and loss. The resort, like the colonizers who had built it, was unmoored—a monument to ambitions that had eroded under the weight of history, leaving behind only silence and the memory of what had been.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: Excerpt1 better fits the original excerpt. Excerpt2 struggles to maintain an objective or coherent tone and stumbles repeatedly, in nearly every sentence, into overwrought imagery, description, and alliteration ("the weight of its past in every crumbling façade and every shattered tile strewn across the once-immaculate promenade"; "discarded detritus of another era—splintered furniture, faded paperbacks, and Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot"; "the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow "; etc.) that the original excerpt avoids. While paragraph1 struggles somewhat to maintain a clear history of the place it depicts for its reader, it avoids this sort of language and does create a specific scenic example through the way the teenagers engage with the old resort. This is much more convincing than the vagueness of paragraph2.

written_by_Hank.Original: “Try this one,” said Jack, “and I’ll say it just one time. Tell you what, we could a had a good life together, a fuckin real good life. You wouldn’t do it, Ennis, so what we got now is Brokeback Mountain. Everything built on that. It’s all we got, boy, fuckin all, so I hope you know that if you don’t never know the rest. Count the damn few times we been together in twenty years. Measure the fuckin short leash you keep me on, then ask me about Mexico and then tell me you’ll kill me for needin it and not hardly never gettin it. You got no fuckin idea how bad it gets. I’m not you. I can’t make it on a couple a high-altitude fucks once or twice a year. You’re too much for me, Ennis, you son of a whoreson bitch. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Like vast clouds of steam from thermal springs in winter the years of things unsaid and now unsayable—admissions, declarations, shames, guilts, fears—rose around them. Ennis stood as if heart-shot, face grey and deep-lined, grimacing, eyes screwed shut, fists clenched, legs caving, hit the ground on his knees.“Jesus,” said Jack. “Ennis?” But before he was out of the truck, trying to guess if it was heart attack or the overflow of an incendiary rage, Ennis was back on his feet and somehow, as a coat hanger is straightened to open a locked car and then bent again to its original shape, they torqued things almost to where they had been, for what they’d said was no news. Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt1: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_Hank.Excerpt2: Jack leaned against the post, his chest heaving, words spilling out in a torrent, raw as the gouged earth beneath his boots. “I can’t do this anymore, Ennis. It ain’t just the damn mountain. You hold me like I’m some stray dog on a leash, pullin’ me close when you want and kickin’ me away when you don’t. Ain’t a life, this. Not for me.” His voice cracked, ricocheted into the dry air. “Wish I knew how to quit you, but it’s like tryin’ to wrench a fishhook outta your own throat.” He tipped his hat back, his eyes watery but fierce, daring the other man to respond. Ennis stood frozen, fists tight, the sinews of his neck stretched taut like old barbed wire. When the words hit their mark, it was like a shot fired too close—he crumpled, knees buckling, gasping for air as though Jack’s truths had knocked it clean out of him. “Jesus,” Jack muttered, rushing forward, unsure if he should steady Ennis or step away. The distance between them felt insurmountable, a chasm carved out of years of furtive touches and unspoken words. For a moment, there was only the rasp of their breath, mingling with the faint hum of crickets and the whisper of dry grass. Ennis lifted his head, the shadows on his face deep, his expression unreadable. He staggered to his feet, brushing off Jack’s hand, and the weight of their shared silence pressed in. Nothing was mended, no path forward uncovered. Just the same cycle of longing and restraint, heartbreak hanging in the air like steam from a kettle left too long on the flame, inevitable and unyielding, rising but never dispersing.
written_by_Hank.Reason: Option 2 is much closer. It captures the emotional intensity and physicality of the original, the sense of something raw and uncontainable breaking through. Some of the language is a little more polished than Proulx’s, but the tone is right: restrained and devastating. The original includes lines like: “Count the damn few times we been together in twenty years... You’re too much for me, Ennis, you son of a whoreson bitch. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Option 2 preserves this core emotion in: “Wish I knew how to quit you, but it’s like tryin’ to wrench a fishhook outta your own throat.” And the reaction – “Ennis stood as if heart-shot… hit the ground on his knees” – is mirrored in Option 2: “he crumpled, knees buckling, gasping for air.” Option 1 feels too flattened and staged; lines like “You the storm that stranded me here,” or “a cold distant man making a scene on the roadside,” feel a little theatrical. It loses the lyricism and the silence. Option 2 leans into conflict without resolving it, which is the point.

written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt1: Jack stood there, fists balled in his jacket pockets, words tearing out of him like barbed wire through flesh. "Twenty years we been at this, En. Twenty goddamn years of sneakin up here like outlaws, like we done somethin wrong. You got me on this short leash, always yankin me back when I get too close to somethin real. Christ, I'm sick of it. Sick of these few days we grab like scraps under the table. You think I wanted this half-life? Living off memories of Brokeback till they're wore thin as old leather?" His voice cracked, raw as windburn. "I wish I knew how to quit you." The words hung between them like smoke in still air. Ennis swayed, color draining from his face like water from a broken cup, then his knees buckled and he went down hard on the packed dirt. "Jesus," Jack shouted, lunging forward, thinking heart attack, stroke, something busted loose inside that couldn't be fixed. But Ennis's shoulders were heaving, great gasping sobs tearing out of him, the kind that leave a man hollow. Jack stood frozen, watching his friend shake apart, knowing any touch might shatter what was left. When the storm passed, Ennis climbed to his feet, brushed dirt from his jeans like nothing had happened. They stood in the heavy silence, steam rising between them from their breath in the mountain air, neither looking at the other. Nothing changed. Nothing could change. The moment passed like so many before it, settling into the collection of hurts they carried, weight added to weight until the burden seemed natural as breathing.
written_by_James_Braun.Excerpt2: “I just cain't wrap my head 'round it, Ennis. Just give it to me straight up: you want me around or don't ya? Cause this here between us ain’t anything in full, and because it ain’t anything in full it ain’t hardly anything at all. All we see of each other is here, alone with ourselves. I only got you here. Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Marianne and Connell sit in silence, the weight of their unspoken feelings hanging heavy in the air. Their relationship, once a source of solace and shared dreams, has reached a crossroads. Marianne, ever the observer, has noticed a shift in Connell's behavior. He seems distant, preoccupied, and his eyes hold a flicker of uncertainty that she can't quite decipher. She wonders if she's no longer enough for him. Connell, on the other hand, is grappling with his own internal turmoil. He's aware of the changes within him, the growing sense of responsibility and the desire for a more conventional life. He knows that Marianne is the one person who truly understands him, but he also fears that their relationship is too intense, too consuming. As they sit there, the silence stretches on. Marianne breaks the silence, her voice barely a whisper. What's happening to us? she asks, her eyes searching for answers in Connell's face. He hesitates, unsure of how to articulate his own feelings. I don't know, he finally admits, his voice laced with regret. I think... I think we're growing apart. Marianne nods, her heart sinking. She knows he's right. They've both changed, evolved into different people, and their paths are diverging. Despite the pain, there's a sense of acceptance between them. They understand that this is a natural part of life, that relationships ebb and flow, that sometimes people grow apart. They hold onto the memories of their shared past, the laughter, the intimacy, the love that once bound them together. As they part ways, Marianne and Connell exchange one last lingering glance. There's no bitterness, no resentment, only a deep understanding of what they've lost and what they've gained. They walk away, their hearts heavy but their spirits unbroken. They know that they will always carry a piece of each other within them, a reminder of the love that once bloomed between them.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Reason: Option 2 is the stronger piece. It isn't perfect, but it understands the tone, and is much closer to the original emotionally. The original gives us: “All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room.” Option 2 picks this up directly: “two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions.” The language is more sensitive to contradiction: love and distance, steadiness and insecurity. “A feeling… that there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him.” It allows ambiguity to sit there without needing resolution. written_by_Devin.Excerpt1: Connell said it quietly, his voice catching somewhere in his throat: I wouldn’t have anything without you, you know. Marianne, sitting opposite him, didn’t reply immediately. Her hands were on the table, palms flat, as though grounding herself against the possibility that this was really happening. She thought about the moments when they had each shaped the other in ways small and monumental, like two plants twisting together in the same patch of soil, entwined but separate, their growths inescapably altered by proximity. Connell exhaled sharply, leaning back in his chair as if retreating from his own words. “You’ve done more for me than anyone,” he added, not looking at her now. Marianne felt her chest tighten. She understood what he meant, of course—she’d spent years reflecting on the way they fit together, how they’d softened each other's sharp edges and inadvertently revealed their deepest flaws. And yet, sitting here, she also knew that time had shifted something irreparably between them. He could leave now, and she would still wake up tomorrow. She would still exist. For a long time, she hadn’t believed that. She pressed her fingers against the wood of the table, cool and solid under her touch. “You’ve done a lot for me, too,” she said finally, her voice almost neutral. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.

He hesitates, unsure of how to articulate his own feelings. I don't know, he finally admits, his voice laced with regret. I think... I think we're growing apart. Marianne nods, her heart sinking. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: Marianne sits on the worn leather couch, her fingers absently tracing the cracked armrest while Connell stands by the window, his reflection fragmenting in the rain-spotted glass. The conversation hangs between them like something delicate and inevitable, the kind of moment that will later be dissected in therapy sessions or late-night emails. "I wouldn't have any of this without you," he says, and Marianne notices how he gestures vaguely at nothing in particular, at everything, at the literary magazines on the coffee table, at his MacBook with half-finished submissions to publishing houses. She thinks about how they've grown together, feeding off each other's neuroses and ambitions like some sort of symbiotic organism, each taking what they needed and giving what they could. The irony doesn't escape her - that their relationship, which started in whispered conversations in empty school corridors, had somehow shaped them into people who could write about love and loss in ways that made strangers feel seen. A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo. She doesn't check. Instead, she watches Connell's hands, remembering how they used to nervously adjust his collar during their first readings together at literary festivals. Now they're steady as he explains why he has to leave, using words like 'growth' and 'space' that sound like they've been borrowed from a self-help podcast. The truth is, she's not the same person who needed his validation to feel real anymore. That girl, who used to check his online status compulsively and craft clever responses to his texts, seems like a character in someone else's story now. People change each other, she thinks, that's just what they do, like weather systems colliding and creating something new. She doesn't say this out loud. Instead, she says, "Okay," and watches his reflection blur further in the glass.

written_by_Sophia.Original: Boy, it began to rain like a bastard. In buckets, I swear to God. All the parents and mothers and everybody went over and stood right under the roof of the carrousel, so they wouldn’t get soaked to the skin or anything, but I stuck around on the bench for quite a while. I got pretty soaking wet, especially my neck and my pants. My hunting hat really gave me quite a lot of protection, in a way; but I got soaked anyway. I didn’t care, though. I felt so damn happy all of sudden, the way old Phoebe kept going around and around. I was damn near bawling, I felt so damn happy, if you want to know the truth. I don’t know why. It was just that she looked so damn nice, the way she kept going around and around, in her blue coat and all. God, I wish you could’ve been there.That’s all I’m going to tell about. I could probably tell you what I did after I went home, and how I got sick and all, and what school I’m supposed to go to next fall, after I get out of here, but I don’t feel like it. I really don’t. That stuﬀ doesn’t interest me too much right now.A lot of people, especially this one psychoanalyst guy they have here, keeps asking me if I’m going apply myself when I go back to school next September. It’s such a stupid question, in my opinion. I mean how do you know what you’re going to do till you do it? The answer is, you don’t. I think I am, but how do I know? I swear it’s a stupid question. D.B. isn’t as bad as the rest of them, but he keeps asking me a lot of questions, too. He drove over last Saturday with this English babe that’s in this new picture he’s writing. She was pretty aﬀected, but very good-looking. Anyway, one time when she went to the ladies’ room way the hell down in the other wing D.B. asked me what I thought about all this stuﬀ I just ﬁnished telling you about. I didn’t know what the hell to say. If you want to know the truth, I don’t know what I think about it. I’m sorry I told so many people about it. About all I know is, I sort of miss everybody I told about. Even old Stradlater and Ackley, for instance. I think I even miss that goddam Maurice. It’s funny. Don’t ever tell anybody anything. If you do, you start missing everybody.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt1: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.
written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet. I really didn't. I just stood there with this goofy grin on my face - I probably looked like a complete madman - watching my kid sister in her blue coat having the time of her life. That killed me. It really did. My hunting hat was getting soaked but I didn't care about that either. It's funny, sometimes the things that make you the happiest are the things that get you all sopping wet and probably looking like a complete moron to everybody else. But that's the thing about happiness - it doesn't give a damn what you look like.Now I'm stuck in this crumby place, this rest home or whatever the hell you want to call it, and this hotshot psychoanalyst keeps asking me all these stupid questions about what I'm gonna do with my future. Like if I'm gonna "apply myself" when I go back to school. Jesus Christ, that kills me. These people and their goddam questions. Even old D.B. - he's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still can't help himself. He came to visit me yesterday with this English actress who was sort of beautiful in this fake, Hollywood way. As soon as she went to the bathroom - girls are always going to the bathroom when you're in the middle of something - D.B. starts in with the questions about everything I've been telling him. All about what happened and what I think about it now and all.The funny part is, the more I talk about all this stuff, the more I keep thinking about everybody. Even the people I didn't particularly like, for Chrissake. Like old Stradlater with his secret slob tendencies and Ackley with his pimples and Maurice. I keep thinking about them and missing them, in this crazy way. I don't even know why. I mean, they were all phonies in their own way, but I miss them anyway. That's the thing that drives me crazy in here - how you can hate somebody's guts one minute and then start missing them like hell the next. It's really ironical as hell. Sometimes I think maybe that psychoanalyst isn't so dumb after all, but I'd rather get kicked in the teeth than admit that to him. He'll probably ask me about my violent tendencies next time I see him. That's the trouble with psychoanalysts - they always want to know what everything means, even when things don't mean anything at all.

written_by_Devin.Original: Boy, it began to rain like a bastard. In buckets, I swear to God. written_by_Rachael.Original: Boy, it began to rain like a bastard. In buckets, I swear to God. All the parents and mothers and everybody went over and stood right under the roof of the carrousel, so they wouldn’t get soaked to the skin or anything, but I stuck around on the bench for quite a while. I got pretty soaking wet, especially my neck and my pants. My hunting hat really gave me quite a lot of protection, in a way; but I got soaked anyway. I didn’t care, though. I felt so damn happy all of sudden, the way old Phoebe kept going around and around. I was damn near bawling, I felt so damn happy, if you want to know the truth. I don’t know why. It was just that she looked so damn nice, the way she kept going around and around, in her blue coat and all. God, I wish you could’ve been there.That’s all I’m going to tell about. I could probably tell you what I did after I went home, and how I got sick and all, and what school I’m supposed to go to next fall, after I get out of here, but I don’t feel like it. I really don’t. That stuﬀ doesn’t interest me too much right now.A lot of people, especially this one psychoanalyst guy they have here, keeps asking me if I’m going apply myself when I go back to school next September. It’s such a stupid question, in my opinion. I mean how do you know what you’re going to do till you do it? The answer is, you don’t. I think I am, but how do I know? I swear it’s a stupid question. She was pretty aﬀected, but very good-looking. written_by_Brianna.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.
written_by_Brianna.Excerpt1: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
written_by_Brianna.Excerpt2: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.

written_by_Sophia.Excerpt2: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. Maybe tomorrow one of us will break through, touch the world beyond the fences. Maybe tomorrow the Angels will look back. Maybe tomorrow the tiles will finally add up to freedom.
written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.
written_by_Celeste.Reason: Excerpt1 is closer to the original. It better understands that the transaction being proposed by the narrator with the guards is an exchange ("We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling."), not a plea for mercy, which paragraph2 mistakes it for ("We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt1: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. written_by_Celeste.Excerpt2: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt1: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.
written_by_Yash_Tumbak.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”

written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt1: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
