The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_Devanshi.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.

written_by_James_Cato.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt1: At breakfast, my father handed me an envelope thick with cash, a gesture both startling and unsettling. "For Christmas," he said with forced cheer, his eyes flicking toward Chitra, who was sipping her tea, avoiding my gaze. He added, almost apologetically, “And Disney World, with us. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_James_Cato.Excerpt2: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Original: I am failing as a woman. I am failing as a feminist. To freely accept the feminist label would not be fair to good feminists. If I am, indeed, a feminist, I am a rather bad one. I am a mess of contradictions. There are many ways in which I am doing feminism wrong, at least according to the way my perceptions of feminism have been warped by being a woman.I want to be independent, but I want to be taken care of and have someone to come home to. I have a job I’m pretty good at. I am in charge of things. I am on committees. People respect me and take my counsel. I want to be strong and professional, but I resent how hard I have to work to be taken seriously, to receive a fraction of the consideration I might otherwise receive. Sometimes I feel an overwhelming need to cry at work, so I close my office door and lose it. I want to be in charge and respected and in control, but I want to surrender, completely, in certain aspects of my life. Who wants to grow up? When I drive to work, I listen to thuggish rap at a very loud volume even though the lyrics are degrading to women and offend me to my core. The classic Ying Yang Twins song “Salt Shaker”? It’s amazing. “Bitch you gotta shake it till your camel starts to hurt.”Poetry.(I am mortified by my music choices.)I care what people think.Pink is my favorite color. I used to say my favorite color was black to be cool, but it is pink—all shades of pink. If I have an accessory, it is probably pink. I read Vogue, and I’m not doing it ironically, though it might seem that way. I once live-tweeted the September issue. I demonstrate little outward evidence of this, but I have a very indulgent fantasy where I have a closet full of pretty shoes and purses and matching outfits. I love dresses. For years I pretended I hated them, but I don’t. Maxi dresses are one of the finest clothing items to become popular in recent memory. I have opinions on maxi dresses! I shave my legs! Again, this mortifies me. If I take issue with the unrealistic standards of beauty women are held to, I shouldn’t have a secret fondness for fashion and smooth calves, right?
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.
written_by_Renne_Flory.Excerpt2: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

I crave independence, the freedom to be my own woman, but I also yearn for the comfort of being cared for, of surrendering to vulnerability. I strive for professionalism, to be taken seriously in a world that often dismisses women, but I also want to embrace my femininity, to express myself without fear of judgment.I'm a kaleidoscope of conflicting emotions, a whirlwind of passion and doubt. I'm fiercely independent, yet I long for connection. I'm confident and self-assured, yet I'm plagued by insecurities. I'm a feminist, but I'm also a woman who loves all things pink and sparkly.I oscillate between wanting to burn the system down and simply wanting to find my place within it. I rail against the patriarchy, yet I find myself drawn to men who embody traditional masculinity. I champion body positivity, yet I struggle with my own body image.I'm a walking contradiction, a living embodiment of the complexities of womanhood. I'm not sure what it all means, this jumble of contradictions that makes up who I am. But I'm learning to embrace it, to accept that I can be both a feminist and a woman who loves fashion, both independent and vulnerable, both confident and insecure.I'm a work in progress, a constant evolution of self-discovery. I'm not perfect, but I'm perfectly me. And in a world that demands conformity, that's my own small act of rebellion.I'm not sure what the future holds, but I'm excited to find out. I'm excited to continue to grow and learn and evolve as a woman, a feminist, and a human being. I'm excited to continue to challenge myself, to push the boundaries of what it means to be a woman in today's world.I'm excited to continue to find my voice, to speak my truth, even when it's messy and complicated. I'm excited to continue to embrace my contradictions, to celebrate the beautiful mess that I am.
written_by_Ashni.Excerpt2: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.
